title: Don't rewrite IPython help syntax and prompts in notebooks
body:
### Description

To format a notebook cell with magics in it, Black runs IPython's `TransformerManager` on the cell, masks the `get_ipython()` calls it produces and turns them back into magics afterwards. IPython also rewrites some syntax that can't be turned back into what was written, and Black then put IPython's version into the cell:

- help after an object, `pd.read_csv?` / `df.head??`, became `?pd.read_csv` / `??df.head` (and `%pinfo obj` became `?obj`)
- wildcard searches such as `str.*find*?` became `%psearch str.*find*`
- a pasted `>>>` or `In [1]:` session lost its prompts
- the autocall escapes `/f a` and `,f a b` became `f(a)` and `f("a", "b")`

Reproduction on main (`9485ad4`), same with 26.10.1:

```console
$ cat > repro.ipynb <<'NB'
{"cells":[
 {"cell_type":"code","execution_count":null,"metadata":{},"outputs":[],"source":["pd.read_csv?"]},
 {"cell_type":"code","execution_count":null,"metadata":{},"outputs":[],"source":["str.*find*?"]},
 {"cell_type":"code","execution_count":null,"metadata":{},"outputs":[],"source":[">>> import math\n",">>> math.sqrt(2)"]}
],"metadata":{"language_info":{"name":"python"}},"nbformat":4,"nbformat_minor":5}
NB
$ black --diff repro.ipynb
--- repro.ipynb	...:cell_0
+++ repro.ipynb	...:cell_0
@@ -1 +1 @@
-pd.read_csv?
+?pd.read_csv
--- repro.ipynb	...:cell_1
+++ repro.ipynb	...:cell_1
@@ -1 +1 @@
-str.*find*?
+%psearch str.*find*
--- repro.ipynb	...:cell_2
+++ repro.ipynb	...:cell_2
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
->>> import math
->>> math.sqrt(2)
+import math
+
+math.sqrt(2)
would reformat repro.ipynb
```

IPython runs both versions the same way, but Black shouldn't rewrite what the user typed, and `len?` or `str.*find*?` cells are common in teaching notebooks. With this change the file is left unchanged.

`mask_cell` now checks that putting the masked magics back gives the original cell, ignoring indentation and surrounding whitespace (IPython strips those anyway), and raises `NothingChanged` if it doesn't, like Black already does for multi-line magics. This replaces the old line count check, which only caught multi-line magics. Help before the object (`?obj`), other line and cell magics and indented cells are formatted as before.

`test_set_input` expected `a = b??` to become `??b`, which drops the `a = `. That expectation was set in #3008 when IPython 8.3 changed how it transforms the line; before that, the cell was left alone. It's left alone again now on every IPython version, so the version skip and the `IPython` import it needed are removed.

Tests: `test_rewritten_ipython_syntax_noop` covers help and source after the object, a wildcard search, both prompt styles and the two autocall escapes. It fails on main. `tox -e py` passes (639 passed, 1 skipped, plus 96 jupyter tests), and so do `tox -e run_self` and `pre-commit run -a`. The notebook tests also pass with IPython 8.2.0. Formatting the 2,176 code cells of 218 notebooks from other projects gives identical output on main and on this branch.

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (No style change, Black now leaves these cells alone.)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (Added this case to the lists of skipped cells in the Jupyter guide and the FAQ.)

title: Keep IPython magics in annotated assignments in notebooks
body:
### Description

IPython transforms an assignment magic that has a type annotation the same way as a plain one, so in a notebook cell

```python
files: list[str] = !ls *.csv
```

runs as `files: list[str] = get_ipython().getoutput('ls *.csv')`. `MagicFinder` only visited `ast.Assign` nodes, so the magic in an annotated assignment was never masked, and Black wrote the transformed call back into the cell.

Reproduction on `main` (`f74dfd7`):

```console
$ cat > repro.ipynb <<'NB'
{"cells":[{"cell_type":"code","execution_count":null,"metadata":{},"outputs":[],"source":["files: list[str] = !ls *.csv\n","print(files)"]}],"metadata":{"language_info":{"name":"python"}},"nbformat":4,"nbformat_minor":5}
NB
$ black repro.ipynb
reformatted repro.ipynb
```

The cell now reads `files: list[str] = get_ipython().getoutput("ls *.csv")`. The same happens for `home: str = %env HOME`. With this change the file is left unchanged.

title: Fix crash on two `# fmt: skip` statements in a row
body:
### Description

Two statements in a row that each have `# fmt: skip` inside a bracket crash Black:

```python
foo(a  # fmt: skip
)
bar(b  # fmt: skip
)
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 2:1" because the output is `)bar(b  # fmt: skip`. The same happens when the second statement is a `with`, `if`, `for`, `class`, decorator or `return` whose first line is hidden, e.g. `x = (  # fmt: skip` ... `)` followed by `with (  # fmt: skip` ... `):`. This is a regression from #5610 and isn't in a release yet: 26.10.1 formats these fine.

#5610 keeps hidden code on the line where the previous hidden code ends when there is no newline in its prefix, for two `# fmt: skip` brackets in one statement. But the newline between two statements isn't in the prefix of the second one, it's in the `NEWLINE` token of the first. When `# fmt: skip` hides a whole statement, that token is hidden with it too, so nothing separates the two hidden parts anymore. And when the second statement is a compound statement, its keyword is hidden, so `visit_stmt` doesn't start a new line before it.

`_continues_fmt_skip_line` now also checks that the hidden code doesn't start a statement. Hidden code that continues the previous one's line always comes after something in the same statement, like the `if` of a conditional expression, or the `;` it hides along with the next statement.

I checked ~18k generated combinations of two or three statements (with brackets hidden in different ways, one-liners, `;`, `# fmt: off`, comments and blank lines, at module level and in a function) in stable, preview and unstable. Wherever `main` doesn't crash, the output is the same with this branch, and none of them crash now.

title: Fix crash when a comment and a `# type: ignore` are joined onto one line
body:
### Description

Black crashes when it joins a line that ends in a comment with the next line, that line ends in `# type: ignore`, and nothing is left to split. A keyword argument, a parameter default or a dict value whose value comes after a comment is enough:

```python
parser.add_argument(
    "--foo",
    default=  # keep in sync with bar
        DEFAULT_FOO,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
)
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.1 on Python (CPython) 3.13.5 produced code that is not equivalent to the source.  Please report a bug on https://github.com/psf/black/issues.  This diff might be helpful: /tmp/blk_....log
```

The AST diff is one missing `TypeIgnore`. Black renders the two comments in source order, `default=DEFAULT_FOO,  # keep in sync with bar  # type: ignore[arg-type]`, and Python only recognizes a `# type: ignore` at the start of a comment. With `--fast` that line is written out and mypy reports the `arg-type` error again. `**  # comment` followed by `kwargs,  # type: ignore[...]`, and `"key":  # comment` followed by a dict value, crash the same way. Both 26.10.1 and main are affected.

This makes `Line.__str__` render a line's `# type: ignore` comments before its other comments:

```python
parser.add_argument(
    "--foo",
    default=DEFAULT_FOO,  # type: ignore[arg-type]  # keep in sync with bar
)
```

mypy accepts a comment after `# type: ignore[...]`, so the ignore keeps working. A separate `# type: ignore` after another comment on one output line was always lost before, so only output that used to crash changes, and an already formatted file can't contain one. On the 263 files of CPython's `Lib/` and a venv's site-packages that contain `# type: ignore`, main and this branch give identical output in stable and preview. I also formatted 60,000 snippets made by inserting a `# note` and a `# type: ignore[misc]` into CPython code: in stable mode 868 crash on main and 866 of those format now (the other 2 put the comment before the `:` of an annotation and still crash), and no snippet that formats on main changes.

This is separate from #5618, which keeps the comments of an attribute chain on their own lines. That is the better layout for chains, and with both changes applied both test cases pass.

title: Fix crash on a multi-line parenthesized tuple target
body:
### Description

Since #5606, Black crashes on a tuple target that is split over lines inside parentheses when the assignment doesn't fit on one line. Black 26.10.0 and `main` before #5606 format these fine. From attrs (`attr/_make.py`), with `--skip-magic-trailing-comma`:

```python
if props.added_pickling:
    (
        self._cls_dict["__getstate__"],
        self._cls_dict["__setstate__"],
    ) = self._make_getstate_setstate()
```

```
error: cannot format x.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced different code on the second pass of the formatter.
```

Without the trailing comma it happens with the default options too:

```python
if x:
    (self._cls_dict["__getstate__"],
     self._cls_dict["__setstate__"]) = self._make_getstate_setstate()
```

The first run splits the last subscript of the target:

```python
if x:
    self._cls_dict["__getstate__"], self._cls_dict[
        "__setstate__"
    ] = self._make_getstate_setstate()
```

A second run then gives what the assignment written without parentheses gives:

```python
if x:
    self._cls_dict["__getstate__"], self._cls_dict["__setstate__"] = (
        self._make_getstate_setstate()
    )
```

#5606 replaces the target's atom with its content once the target's parentheses are invisible, so that it splits like a target written without parentheses. But a tuple target written without parentheses gets invisible parentheses too (the `testlist_star_expr` at the start of the statement is wrapped in them), and they affect the split. The right-hand split that omits the optional parentheses around the value stops at them instead of going into the target, and `_prefer_split_rhs_oop_over_rhs` counts them as brackets on the left-hand side. So for a tuple, dropping the atom makes the target split differently from one written without parentheses, which is what the next pass sees.

The first version of #5606 kept the atom for tuple targets. That exception was removed in review because no input showed a difference, and these inputs do. This change puts it back: a tuple target keeps its invisible parentheses, and other targets are unwrapped as before.

I found this by running Black over the site-packages of my local virtualenvs (39,391 files). With `--skip-magic-trailing-comma` it crashes on attrs `_make.py`, moto `route53/responses.py` and `ssoadmin/responses.py`, and PyTorch `_dynamo/polyfills/pytree.py`. With `--line-length 40` it crashes on three docutils files that have `(node.source,\n node.line) = self.state_machine.get_source_and_line(self.lineno)`. With this change they all format, in stable and preview, and the output is the same as on `main` before #5606 (976bbe4). This branch formats all 1,281 files in that corpus that have a parenthesized tuple target without errors, in stable, preview, `--line-length 40` and `--skip-magic-trailing-comma`. I also ran 864 of them on `main`. Apart from the crashes above, the only difference is `(self.typeid, self.address, self.id) = (typeid, address, id)` in billiard's and multiprocess's `managers.py` with `--line-length 40`. Since #5606, `main` splits the value of that line too, and with this change it is formatted as it was before #5606.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (A crash fix for a change that isn't released yet. Tuple targets format as they did before #5606.)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary? (#5606 isn't released yet, so I added this PR's number to its entry, like #5612 did for #5597.)
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary? (The two examples above, in `remove_parens_from_lhs.py` and `skip_magic_trailing_comma.py`. Both fail on `main`, which gives the split subscript.)

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` on a nested bracket after `with` or `yield`
body:
### Description

`# fmt: skip` on an opening bracket crashes Black when the bracket starts an operand that's nested inside a longer expression after `with` or `yield`:

```python
with (  # fmt: skip
    a
) == 1 and b:
    pass
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 1:4". The same happens with `) + 1 == 2:`, `with not (  # fmt: skip` ... `) or b:`, `async with`, and `with ... as c`. After `yield` the output still parses but means something else (`yield` ends up on its own line), so Black reports "produced code that is not equivalent to the source". 26.10.1 crashes on these too.

To find the code before the bracket on the same line, the walk in `_generate_ignored_nodes_from_fmt_skip` climbs to the parent when a node has no previous sibling, but only by one level. Here the bracket is the first leaf of a `comparison` inside an `and_test`, so the walk stops at the `comparison` and `with` is never added to the skipped line. The skipped code then becomes a standalone comment after `with`, which gets split onto its own line.

Both climbs (the one before the walk and the one inside it) now keep going up while the node is the first child of its parent. The inner loop that collapsed fully ignored parents is folded into the outer one, since it did the same climb with an extra condition.

With the whole line skipped, a unary operator before the bracket can be hidden while its operand goes on after the closing bracket (`with -(  # fmt: skip` ... `).y and b:`). That leaves a `factor` node with only the operand, so `visit_factor` now checks the number of children instead of unpacking two.

In other statements this didn't crash, but the line wasn't kept as is either. For example `x = (  # fmt: skip` ... `) == 1 and b` was turned into `x = (` followed by the bracket on its own line. Those lines are now left unchanged. Code that was already formatted by Black stays the same: I ran ~19k generated variants (`x =`, `return`, `yield`, `with`, `if`, `assert`, lambdas, unary operators, trailers, and/or/comparison/arithmetic operands) and the output of `main` for each one is unchanged with this branch, in stable, preview and unstable. None of them crash now.

title: Keep walrus parentheses in subscripts for Python 3.9 and older targets
body:
### Description

With `--preview`, Black removes the parentheses around a walrus that is the whole subscript, even when the target versions include Python 3.8 or 3.9:

```python
# input, works on Python 3.8
x[(y := 1)]

# output with `black --preview -t py38`
x[y := 1]
```

Python 3.8 and 3.9 can't parse the output: an unparenthesized named expression in a subscript is only allowed from Python 3.10 (in the 3.9 grammar, `slice` takes an `expression`; 3.10 changed it to `named_expression`, and `pep_572_py310.py` notes this too). Black still exits with 0, and the safety check doesn't catch it because Black itself runs on 3.10 or newer. The same happens with auto-detection and with `requires-python = ">=3.8"`, since a walrus makes Black infer 3.8 as the lowest target.

This comes from the new `remove_redundant_subscript_parentheses` preview feature (#5496). The fix follows #5502, which fixed the same problem for set literals: it adds a feature for 3.10 and newer, and `maybe_make_parens_invisible_in_atom()` keeps the parentheses around a walrus in a subscript when the targets include 3.9 or older. Extra parentheses are still removed, so `x[((y := 1))]` becomes `x[(y := 1)]`, and the other redundant parentheses in subscripts are removed as before. For 3.10+ targets the output doesn't change.

The new `preview_walrus_in_subscript_py38` case fails without this change, and `preview_walrus_in_subscript_py310` shows that 3.10+ targets still drop the parentheses. `pytest tests` passes (I skipped `test_blackd.py` since I didn't install the `d` extra), and so do `black --check`, flake8 with flake8-bugbear, and mypy on the changed files.

title: Fix crash on a type: ignore chain with another comment between the ignores
body:
### Description

#5297 keeps the `# type: ignore` comments of a method chain on separate lines. With another comment between two of them, Black still fails:

```python
def _get_light_style(app: sphinx.application.Sphinx) -> Style:
    return (
        app  # type: ignore[no-any-return]
            .builder  # comment
            .highlighter  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
            .formatter_args["style"]
        )
```

```
error: cannot format x.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced code that is not equivalent to the source.
```

The AST diff is one missing `TypeIgnore`. `type_ignore_comment_split` ends a line only after a `# type: ignore`, so it produces `app  # type: ignore[no-any-return]` and then `.builder.highlighter  # comment  # type: ignore[attr-defined]`. A `# type: ignore` written after another comment on the same line is not a type ignore any more (Python only recognizes it at the start of a comment), so the safety check rejects the output. The same happens with the regular comment before the first `# type: ignore` (`app  # comment` / `.builder  # type: ignore` / `.highlighter  # type: ignore`).

`type_ignore_comment_split` now ends the line after every comment in the chain, not only after a `# type: ignore`:

```python
def _get_light_style(app: sphinx.application.Sphinx) -> Style:
    return (
        app  # type: ignore[no-any-return]
        .builder  # comment
        .highlighter  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        .formatter_args["style"]
    )
```

This only changes the output when a regular comment comes before a `# type: ignore` in the same segment, and that output always lost the type ignore, so code that formats today formats the same. I checked that on the 988 files of a 13,067-file corpus (CPython stdlib, site-packages, several projects) that contain `# type: ignore`: the output is identical on `main` and on this branch, in stable and preview.

I found this by inserting `# comment` after random tokens of Black's own test cases and formatting in safe mode.

- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?

title: Simplify how we preserve skipped code and comments
body:
This is a refactor of some recent code, no behaviour change is intended

Black remembers the first token of a skipped block so it can tell, for example, whether a skipped import belongs with the imports above it. Cloning the block used to copy that token and its parent subtree. Reuse the original token and share one immutable set of selected lines across clones.

Keep each comment's original line and its distance from the token it precedes. This lets --line-ranges locate the comment without scanning the prefix again. When preserving a comment's indentation, account for the indent the renderer adds so formatting the same range twice doesn't move the comment.

Co-authored-by Codex

title: Fix an own-line fmt: skip after a blank line skipping the statement above it
body:
### Description

A `# fmt: skip` comment on a line of its own is meant to skip nothing (`fmtskip4.py`: `a =   2` followed by `# fmt: skip` still becomes `a = 2`). But when a blank line comes before it, it skips the statement above instead, and that statement is merged with the comment:

```python
x = 1

# foo  # fmt: skip
```

becomes `x = 1\n# foo  # fmt: skip\n` (the blank line is removed), and in the middle of a file an extra blank line can appear instead. After an import it never settles:

```python
import a
# foo  # fmt: skip

```

```
error: cannot format x.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced different code on the second pass of the formatter.
```

The first pass adds the blank line after the import, which turns the comment into the "after a blank line" case, so the second pass merges `import a` with it and removes the blank line again. 26.10.1 behaves the same.

The cause is `_is_valid_standalone_fmt_comment`: it accepts every comment on its own line before checking anything else, which is right for `# fmt: off` but lets `# fmt: skip` through too, so the check below it (a `# fmt: skip` whose previous leaf is a `NEWLINE`/`INDENT`/`DEDENT` is ignored) never runs for it. A comment directly on a line of its own (no blank line before it) never had this problem, because it isn't a standalone comment and reaches that check. Own-line `# fmt: skip` comments between statements are now ignored too. Inside brackets, where the previous leaf is an opening bracket or another token, nothing changes (`fmtskip_in_parens.py`, `fmtskip_after_bracket_with_comment.py`).

I found this by appending `# fmt: skip` to random lines of a 37,025-file corpus (CPython stdlib, site-packages, Ruff fixtures) and formatting in safe mode: 6 of the failing files in a 6,000-file run were this case, and they format with this change. Formatting the 162 corpus files that already contain `# fmt: skip` or `# fmt: off` gives byte-identical output on `main` and this branch, in stable and preview.

- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary? (`fmtskip_own_line_between_statements.py`, after a blank line at module level and before a method; it fails on `main`.)

title: Keep empty lines before comments outside --line-ranges
body:
### Description

With `--line-ranges`, the empty lines before a comment that is in the prefix of an unselected statement were still capped like those of formatted code: to two at module level and to one in a block. For example, with `--line-ranges=7-7`,

```python
x = 1



# comment
y = 2
z  =  3
```

becomes

```python
x = 1


# comment
y = 2
z = 3
```

so formatting line 7 also removes one of the empty lines 2–4. Without the comment, the three empty lines are kept: since #5175, the empty lines before an unselected statement aren't capped and the comments in its prefix keep their formatting, but those comments become lines of their own, and `EmptyLineTracker` caps the empty lines before them.

This change marks the comments that `generate_comments()` keeps as they are, by setting `line_ranges_selected` on them, and `_maybe_empty_lines()` doesn't cap the empty lines before such a comment, as it doesn't for an unselected statement. The other empty line rules still apply: after a selected `def`, for instance, an unselected comment still gets two empty lines before it, like an unselected statement.

I found this by formatting random line ranges of the Python 3.14 standard library and looking for changed lines outside the ranges. For example, `black --line-ranges=109-122` on `Lib/asyncio/tools.py` removes one of the three empty lines before the `# ─── indexing helpers ───` comment on line 27 and changes nothing else; with this change, it leaves the file unchanged. Of the 212 results that changed lines outside the ranges and the statements that overlap them (4 random sets of ranges per file, in the stable and preview styles), 92 no longer do with this change, and none changes such a line that it didn't change before. Most of the others remove empty lines at the start of the file, before an unselected first statement; I left that alone, since `test_line_ranges_removed_at_start_of_file_stay_unformatted` expects it.

The new `line_ranges_preserve_blank_lines_before_comments` case checks a comment at module level and one in a class body, and fails without this change. `pytest tests` passes (I skipped `test_blackd.py` since I didn't install the `d` extra), and so do `black --check`, flake8 with flake8-bugbear, and mypy on the changed files.

title: Fix crash on a fmt: skip line that closes an earlier bracket and opens another
body:
### Description

Black crashes when the `# fmt: skip` line closes a bracket that was opened on an earlier line and opens one that it doesn't close, for example a return annotation after a multi-line parameter list:

```python
def f(
    a,
) -> A[B  # fmt: skip
]:
    pass
```

```
error: cannot format x.py: Unable to match a closing bracket to the following opening bracket: ]
```

The same happens in methods, `async def` and decorated functions, in stable and preview. 26.10.1 behaves the same.

The skip collects the leaves on the comment's line, here `)`, `->`, `A`, `[` and `B`. When those leave a bracket open, `_generate_ignored_nodes_from_fmt_skip` already keeps the whole enclosing statement instead (the `from x import (  # fmt: skip` case), but it measured that with the net bracket depth. The `)` that closes the parameter list cancels the `[`, so the depth is 0, only the line is converted, and the `]` on the next line has no opening bracket left. The check now counts the opening brackets that stay unclosed, so a closing bracket that belongs to an earlier line no longer cancels one, and the statement is kept as written.

Lines whose brackets were balanced or only left open before are counted the same as before. Formatting the 162 files with `# fmt: skip` or `# fmt: off` from a 37,025-file corpus (CPython stdlib, site-packages, Ruff fixtures) gives byte-identical output on `main` and this branch, in stable and preview. I found this by inserting `# fmt: skip` into Black's test cases and formatting them in safe mode.

- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?

title: Fix crash on two `# fmt: skip` brackets in the same statement
body:
### Description

Two `# fmt: skip` comments on opening brackets in the same statement crash Black when the second one starts on the line where the first bracket closes:

```python
x = a if (  # fmt: skip
    b
) else (  # fmt: skip
    c
)
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 3:1". The same happens with `x = (  # fmt: skip` ... `) if (  # fmt: skip` ... `) else c`, after `return`, in an `if` header, and so on. With a binary operator it's worse, since the output still parses but means something else: `w = (  # fmt: skip` ... `) + (  # fmt: skip` ... `)` turns the second part into a separate `+(b)` statement and Black reports "produced code that is not equivalent to the source". 26.10.1 crashes on all of these.

Each `# fmt: skip` turns its line into a standalone comment, so the statement ends up with two of them in a row. Outside of brackets, `visit_STANDALONE_COMMENT` always starts a new line before a standalone comment, which puts `) else (  # fmt: skip` on its own line. `_force_standalone_comment_split` does the same, since #5538 only lets code (not another standalone comment) follow hidden code that ends in code.

This adds a check for that case: the next standalone comment is code hidden by `# fmt: skip` (not a `# fmt: off` block or code left alone by `--line-ranges`), it doesn't start on a new line, and the previous hidden code ends in code rather than a comment. When it holds, the two parts stay on the same line and the original spacing between them is kept.

`visit_test` also needed a small change. When the `if` part of a conditional is hidden, the `test` node starts with the standalone comment rather than the `if` leaf, so the check from #5586 didn't see it and the conditional was still wrapped in invisible parentheses that later became visible.

title: Fix invalid output for `# fmt: skip` on a short line length
body:
With preview features enabled and a short `--line-length`, Black emits code it cannot parse for a `# fmt: skip` on the opening bracket of a collection used as a binary operand:

```python
y = {  # fmt: skip
    "a": 1} | {"b": 2}
```

`black.format_str(src, mode=black.Mode(preview=True, line_length=30))` fails with `INTERNAL ERROR: ... produced invalid code` and dumps a first pass that ends with a top-level line starting ` | {`:

```
y = {  # fmt: skip
    "a": 1}
 | {
    "b": 2
}
```

Stable formatting of the same input is fine, and so is preview at the default line length, which is why `tests/data/cases/fmtskip_opening_bracket_split.py` (from #5538) does not catch it.

### Cause

The second-opinion pass in `run_transformer` (`FORCE_OPTIONAL_PARENTHESES`) duplicates the line with `append_leaves`. That function builds a fresh `Leaf` and copies `lineno`, but not the `fmt_pass_converted_first_leaf` marker that identifies `fmt: skip`/`fmt: off` code carried in a `STANDALONE_COMMENT`. On the duplicated line the marker is `None`, so `_is_fmt_pass_converted_ending_in_code` no longer recognizes that the hidden code ends in code rather than a comment, and `_force_standalone_comment_split` splits before the `|`, leaving the operator at the start of an unparenthesized line.

### Fix

Copy the marker when `append_leaves` duplicates a leaf.

### Test

`tests/data/cases/fmtskip_opening_bracket_split_short_line.py` runs the input above with `--preview --line-length 30`. It fails on `main` with the `INTERNAL ERROR` and passes with the change.

`pytest tests/test_format.py` → 296 passed. The full `pytest tests/` (excluding `tests/test_blackd.py`, which needs the `d` extra) → 586 passed, 3 failed; the two color tests fail identically on an unmodified checkout, and `test_schema_entrypoint` failed in the full run but passes when run alone, so none of them is related to this change.

A CHANGES.md entry will follow with the PR number.

title: Fix crash on a multi-line parenthesized assignment target
body:
### Description

Black crashes on this assignment from matplotlib (`backends/backend_cairo.py`):

```python
def restore_region(surface, region, sly, slx, sh, sw):
    (np.frombuffer(surface.get_data(), np.uint32)
     .reshape((sh, sw))[sly, slx]) = region._data
```

```
error: cannot format x.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced different code on the second pass of the formatter.
```

It fails in stable and preview, and 26.10.1 behaves the same. Written on one line, `(np.frombuffer(...).reshape((sh, sw))[sly, slx]) = region._data` formats fine.

Since #4865, the parentheses around a target that is split over lines are kept (`_is_atom_multiline`), so the first pass joins the target onto one line inside them and wraps the value in parentheses. On the next pass, the now single-line target's parentheses are made invisible, but the invisible-paren atom stays around it. A single pass formats `(target) = value` differently from `target = value`: with the atom, the value stays wrapped. Without it, the subscript is split. `format_str`'s second internal pass hides this for a target written on one line, but a multi-line one needs a third pass, so the stability check fails.

When the target's parentheses become invisible, the atom is now replaced by its content, so the target splits like one written without parentheses. An atom with a comment inside keeps it (otherwise `(a.b  # c\n) = 1` would lose the comment), and the atom's prefix moves to the target (otherwise blank lines before the statement would be dropped).

I found this by running Black over a 37,025-file corpus (CPython stdlib, site-packages, Ruff fixtures). This was the only file with a non-tuple target in redundant parentheses, and it now formats. For 400 random files from the corpus plus this one, the output on `main` and on this branch is identical apart from the crash, in stable and preview. Inserting comments around parenthesized targets (40 rounds) gave no crashes with the fix. Other target shapes I tried (a blank line or comment before, `+=`, `(x): int`, `(a) = (b) = 1`, `((a))`, `(*a,)`) format the same as on `main`.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (A crash fix, so stable as the policy allows; code that formatted before formats the same.)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?

- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (Not needed.)

title: Fix crash on a fmt: skip header containing an inner skipped bracket
body:
### Description

A compound statement header with `# fmt: skip` crashes when a bracket inside it has its own `# fmt: skip` on the opening line but not on the closing one:

```python
if (
    a in (  # fmt: skip
        1,
    )
):  # fmt: skip
    pass
```

```
error: cannot format x.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced different code on the second pass of the formatter.
```

With `--fast`, each run adds blank lines before the header's `):`, and a comment after the inner `)` (`)  # foobar`) is moved to its own line. The same happens with `while` and `elif`, and with `-(`, `not (`, `a + (` and similar. A header where the inner `)` also has `# fmt: skip` works; that is the case #5401 fixed. 26.10.1 behaves the same.

The inner `# fmt: skip` turns `a in (  # fmt: skip` ... `)` into a standalone comment whose text ends with the code `)`. When the header's `# fmt: skip` then stringifies the header, `stringify_node` appends a newline to every standalone comment that doesn't end with one, to end its trailing comment (#4872). This one has no trailing comment, and the next leaf (the header's `)`) already starts with its own newline, so the text gets an extra blank line on every pass. The newline is now only added when the last line of the standalone comment has a `#`. A skipped block ending in code is followed by its own source unchanged, so the header stays exactly as written.

I found this by inserting comments into Black's test cases and formatting them in safe mode. Formatting the 162 files with `# fmt: skip` or `# fmt: off` from a 37,025-file corpus (CPython stdlib, site-packages, Ruff fixtures) gives byte-identical output on `main` and this branch, in stable and preview.

title: Fix lambda turned into a tuple by a comment before its parameters
body:
### Description

A standalone comment between `lambda` and its parameters makes Black turn a parenthesized lambda into a tuple:

```python
f = (
    lambda  # comment 1
    # comment 2
    *args, **kwargs: # comment 3
    aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa(*args, **kwargs) + 1
)
```

In safe mode this fails with "produced code that is not equivalent to the source". With `--fast` the output is:

```python
f = (
    lambda  # comment 1
    # comment 2
    *args,
    **kwargs: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa(  # comment 3
        *args, **kwargs
    ),
    +1,
)
```

which is a tuple. 26.10.1 behaves the same.

The standalone comment starts a new line that holds the parameters but not `lambda`, so the bracket tracker never sees the `lambda` that normally hides the parameter commas, and `delimiter_split` splits at them as if they were tuple elements (and then adds a trailing comma). This is close to #5533, where a comment inside a parameter default caused the same tuple, but here the comma that gets split is the parameter separator itself. Like the for-target commas in `is_split_after_delimiter` (#4296), commas whose parent is the `varargslist` of a lambda are now never delimiters.

I found this by running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview): Ruff's `expression/lambda.py` failed in both styles and now formats, with no new failures in the run.

- CHANGES.md: replaced with the suggested wording — PR number only, shorter, no internal vocabulary.
- docs: the feature-list bullet is shortened and the "see below" section is now one short lead-in sentence plus one example; the "already fits / brackets / name so long" assumptions paragraph is gone.
- `visit_argument` and the helpers: one-line docstrings; rule details moved to short comments at the specific code points.
- Wrapping rule redesigned: wrap simply when the argument is over the line length unwrapped and would fit when wrapped; the "line length won back" heuristic and the `name >= 4` gate are gone.
- Value splittability/split points now come from the delimiter machinery (`brackets.is_split_before_delimiter`, the engine wrapped by #4881's `max_delimiter_priority()`); every delimiter-bounded part must fit on its indented line.
- Implicitly concatenated string values are treated like any other value (no special exclusion): they can be parenthesized, but this feature never splits or merges strings — a pure string seam is not registered as a wrap split point, so Black's own seam-splitting (#3497/#5554) stays in charge and `preview_long_strings__regression` keeps its expected output.
- The `syms.argument` carve-out in the walrus guard of `maybe_make_parens_invisible_in_atom` was removed, as verified in review.

The mid-rebase conflicts with main (CHANGES.md, `future_style.md`, `mode.py`, `black.schema.json`) were resolved as unions and the schema stays generated from `mode.py`.

Local verification (Windows 11, Python 3.14, editable install at this main state):
- `pytest tests -q -n auto`: **650 passed, 14 skipped, 62 subtests passed**; `black --check src tests`: clean.
Full CI will re-run on the new head. Prepared with AI assistance (OpenCode, model GLM, autonomous under the account owner's direction); diff and results hand-verified.

---

### Description

Fixes #2893
Closes #5335

When a keyword argument's value is an expression Black cannot split ÔÇö a bare
attribute chain like `long_obj.long_attr`, a plain name, or a literal ÔÇö and the
whole argument exceeds the line length, Black previously had no split point and
left the line too long:

```python
# Before (118 chars)
func(
    long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_arg=long_long_long_long_long_class.long_long_long_long_attr
)
```

Assignment right-hand sides avoid exactly this by being wrapped in (invisible)
parentheses via `parens=ASSIGNMENTS`, so `x = value.attr` splits as
`x = (\n    value.attr\n)`. Keyword arguments (`syms.argument`) had no equivalent,
so their values never got that treatment.

This adds a `visit_argument` hook that wraps such values in (invisible)
parentheses, mirroring assignments ÔÇö but only when it actually helps:

- the value is genuinely **unsplittable** (no brackets anywhere and no
  top-level delimiter, so `right_hand_split`/`delimiter_split` have nothing to
  work with), and
- wrapping can **fit**: the `name=(` head fits within the line length, and the
  name is at least four characters so moving the value to its own line actually
  shortens the overflowing line.

Values that already have a split point (calls, subscripts, collections, binops,
comparisons, string concatenation) are untouched. Arguments whose name alone
already overflows are also left alone, matching the existing behaviour for
assignments.

```python
# After (with --preview)
func(
    long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_long_arg=(
        long_long_long_long_long_class.long_long_long_long_attr
    )
)
```

It also preserves the required parentheses around a walrus in a keyword argument
(`f(x=(y := 1))`), which would otherwise become invalid code.

Because this changes output, it is gated behind the new preview feature
`parenthesize_unsplittable_keyword_arguments`, following the stability policy.
Full test suite passes (659 passed); a fuzz run over ~3000 synthetic inputs and
400 stdlib files produced no invalid, unstable, or crashing output.

- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation?

title: fmt: don't glue statement onto '# fmt: on' line (#5524)
body:
## Summary

`_handle_comment_only_fmt_block()` updated `leaf.prefix` by slicing `original_prefix` at `fmt_on_comment.consumed`. `consumed` counts through the trailing newline of `# fmt: on`, so when `# fmt: on` was the last comment the slice was empty and the next statement got glued onto the directive line:

    # fmt: onTIMEOUT = 30

Keep a bare newline as the prefix so the statement stays on its own line. `generate_comments()` strips a trailing newline from prefixes, so this renders with no blank line.

## Reproducer

`black --line-ranges 7-7` on:

```
# fmt: off
#---------+---------#
#  name   |  value  #
#---------+---------#
# fmt: on
TIMEOUT = 30
retries  =  3
```

previously joined `# fmt: on` and `TIMEOUT = 30` onto one line; now only line 7 is reformatted and `TIMEOUT = 30` survives intact.

## Testing

- `tests/test_format.py`, `tests/test_ranges.py`, `tests/test_black.py`: 531 passed, 12 skipped, 18 subtests passed

Closes #5524, closes #5525

## Standards

- Single change: only `leaf.prefix` handling in `# fmt: on` blocks
- No unrelated code touched; no formatting-only changes
- Full test suite passes; tested against the reported reproducer

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a one-liner whose body starts with a name
body:
### Description

`# fmt: skip` on a one-line compound statement with a semicolon-separated body crashes when the body starts with a bare name:

```python
if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev13+gc3c44ed79 on Python (CPython) 3.14.4 produced invalid code:
cannot parse: example.py:1:8
    if True:if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

The same happens for `while x: a; b`, `for i in r: i; print(i)`, `with a: b; c`, `def f(): x; return x` and `class A: x; y = 1` (26.10.1 too), while `if True: a(); b()` works.

For these one-liners the header is prepended to the skipped nodes (#4800). When the body starts with a bare leaf, the backward walk over the nodes on the line climbs from that leaf to the statement and keeps going, so it already collected the header, and the header was added a second time. This only prepends the header leaves the walk hasn't covered. Checking coverage by leaf matters for `def`, where the walk collects the parameters as one node but the header lists `(` and `)` as leaves.

The new case is `fmtskip_one_liner_bare_name.py`; it fails on `main` with the error above. The full test suite and the pre-commit hooks pass, and running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview) gives the same results as `main`.

Not part of this PR: a block whose only body statement is on its own line is taken for an expanded one-liner and printed as `if True:    a; b  # fmt: skip`, as `main` already does when the body is a call. That is the separate `_find_compound_statement_context` heuristic:

```python
if True:
    a; b  # fmt: skip
```

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (A crash fix, so stable as the policy allows; code that formatted before formats the same.)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (Not needed.)

title: Fix unstable formatting with a comment and an implicitly concatenated last argument
body:
### Description

On `main`, Black fails on this code with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced different code on the second pass of the formatter" and exits with 123:

```python
parser.add_argument("--retries",  # 0 disables
                    help="Number of times to retry "
                         "before giving up")
```

It happens when a comment follows an argument and the last argument is an implicitly concatenated string. The arguments fit on one line inside the call, so the first pass joins them and prints the comment at the end, after the strings. On the next run the comment belongs to the last string, which keeps the strings apart, and the split adds a trailing comma that is printed before the comment. The run after that joins the strings again. With `--skip-magic-trailing-comma` the output is stable, but the comment ends up after the `help=` argument.

`contains_implicit_multiline_string_with_comments` now also returns True when the line ends with an implicitly concatenated string and has a comment anywhere, since joining the line would print that comment right after the strings. The line is then split by delimiter, so the comment stays on the argument it was written after, in both modes:

```python
parser.add_argument(
    "--retries",  # 0 disables
    help="Number of times to retry " "before giving up",
)
```

Already formatted code doesn't change.

Ran: `pytest tests --run-optional no_jupyter`, then the jupyter tests with the extra installed, `black --check .`, isort, flake8 and prettier at the pre-commit versions, and mypy (no new findings).
Checked: about 5,600 CPython 3.14 stdlib statements with a comment injected near an implicit concatenation, and another 5,600 with `# type: ignore` / `# noqa` comments, formatted with and without the patch in default, `-C`, `-l 79/100/120`, preview and unstable modes (the second set without `-l 100` and unstable). Unstable results went from 111 and 91 to 0; the only other changed outputs are 12 and 15 `-C` cases where the comment now stays on its argument. Re-formatting the output of `main` with the patch changes nothing, and about 1,700 stdlib files format identically.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy?
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation?

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` on a bracket followed by `if`/`else`
body:
### Description

`# fmt: skip` on an opening bracket crashes Black when a conditional expression continues after the closing bracket:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) if condition else b
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 4:4". The same happens with `[  # fmt: skip`, with `a if (  # fmt: skip` ... `) else c`, and after `return`, `lambda:` or in a `while` header. 26.5.1 crashes on these too.

The skipped line hides everything up to the closing bracket, including the first operand of the conditional, so the `test` node that's left starts at `if` (or `else`). `visit_test` still wraps it in invisible parentheses, and the right-hand split then makes them visible right after the hidden code:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) (
    if condition else b
)
```

This doesn't reach the `_force_standalone_comment_split` path from #5538, because the split succeeds first. Outside of brackets these parentheses are now left out, so the rest of the expression stays on the closing bracket's line, like `+ [3]` does after #5538. Inside brackets they're kept, so existing output there doesn't change.

A conditional inside brackets that's too long to fit on one line still crashes the same way, since it gets split onto its own line before the parentheses are made visible. That needs a different fix, so I left it out.

title: Keep comments that end a fmt: off region inside brackets verbatim
body:
### Description

Fixes #3372.

Inside brackets, the comments between the end of a `# fmt: off` region and `# fmt: on` get formatted, although they're part of the region. A trailing comment on the last ignored line moves to its own line:

```python
values = _parse_flags(
    # fmt:off
    './program'
    ' --test_config.other_with_default_overitten=True',  # Comment moved
    # fmt:on
)
```

```console
$ black --diff values.py
-    ' --test_config.other_with_default_overitten=True',  # Comment moved
+    ' --test_config.other_with_default_overitten=True',
+    # Comment moved
     # fmt:on
```

Standalone comments there are re-indented. When the region has no `# fmt: on` inside the brackets (the first example in the issue, where `# fmt: on` comes after the closing parenthesis), the comments before the closing bracket are formatted too, so `| np.ndarray               # old API reset` loses its alignment.

**Cause:** `generate_ignored_nodes` stops at the node whose prefix holds `# fmt: on`, or at the end of the bracket's contents. Either way, the comments that end the region are in the prefix of the leaf *after* the last ignored node (the next element or the closing bracket), so `_handle_regular_fmt_block` doesn't put them in the verbatim block.

**Fix:** a new `_take_comments_ending_fmt_off` moves the comments in that leaf's prefix that come before `# fmt: on` into the verbatim block. If the leaf is a closing bracket and there's no `# fmt: on`, it moves all of them. It leaves the last newline in the prefix, so `# fmt: on` or the bracket stays on its own line. It only applies inside brackets. At statement level, the region ends with a `NEWLINE`/`DEDENT`, and the comments before `# fmt: on` are left to the blank-line handling. Moving them there made formatting unstable, and that case doesn't show this bug.

This is a stable-style change, but it only keeps text the user put inside `# fmt: off` unchanged. I checked that formatting the new test input with `main` and then with this branch gives no further changes, so code Black already formatted stays as it is.

New case file `fmtonoff_comments_before_fmt_on.py` covers both examples from the issue, plus trailing and standalone comments before `# fmt: on`, with a closing bracket and with more elements after it, and a nested bracket with no `# fmt: on`. It fails on `main` and passes with the fix. Full test suite: 611 passed, 3 skipped.

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a multi-line `from` import
body:
### Description

`# fmt: skip` on the line that closes a multi-line `from` import crashes Black when another statement follows on that line:

```python
from a import (
    b,
); import c  # fmt: skip
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: 

Oh no! 💥 💔 💥
```

(the message is empty; it is an `AssertionError` from `assert is_rpar_token(parent.children[-1])` in `_normalize_import_from`). 26.10.1 behaves the same.

When collecting the nodes on the skipped line, a closing bracket is widened to its whole bracketed node for atoms and, since #5522, trailers. An import's parentheses are children of the `import_from` node itself, so only `)` was hidden while `(` stayed in the import, and the import normalization then found no `)` to match. This widens the closing parenthesis of an `import_from` too, so the whole import is left alone, like the call in #5522.

I found this by running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview): Ruff's `fmt_skip/top_level_semicolon.py` crashed in both styles and now formats, with no new failures in the run.

Separately, while checking this I saw that a block whose only body statement has a semicolon and `# fmt: skip` is treated as an expanded one-liner and also fails (on `main` and 26.10.1):

```python
if True:
    a; b  # fmt: skip
```

That is a different code path (`_find_compound_statement_context`), so it is not part of this PR; the new test keeps the import in blocks with more than one statement.

title: Fix crash on bytes literals containing \u, \U or \N{...}
body:
### Description

The escape normalization from #2916 also runs on bytes literals, where `\u`, `\U` and `\N{...}` are not escape sequences but plain characters. Changing their case changes the bytes value, so Black fails on valid code:

```python
x = b'{"name": "é"}'   # JSON stored as bytes
y = b"\N{bullet}"
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced code that is not equivalent to the source.
$ black --fast example.py   # silently changes the values
x = b'{"name": "é"}'
y = b"\N{BULLET}"
```

This only normalizes `\x` in bytes literals, which is an escape sequence there and keeps its value. Strings, raw strings and f-strings are unchanged.

I found this by running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview): `ruff/expression/bytes.py` hit the error above in both styles, and with this change it formats without errors. The run reports no new failures.

title: Respect --skip-source-first-line when formatting stdin
body:
### Description

`--skip-source-first-line` (`-x`) is honoured when formatting files by path, but it is silently ignored when the code is passed through stdin (`black -x -`). Instead, the first line is formatted along with the rest. When that line isn't valid Python, which is the case the option exists for (e.g. a Windows batch wrapper), Black fails to parse it:

```console
$ printf '@echo off && python -x "%%~f0" %%* && goto :eof\nx=1\n' | black -x -
error: cannot parse: -:1:6
```

The same file formatted by path works. With `--diff`/`--check` on stdin, an unformatted first line also shows up as a change and makes the check fail.

`format_file_in_place()` splits the header off before decoding and prepends it again afterwards, but `format_stdin_to_stdout()` never looked at `mode.skip_source_first_line`. It now does the same. This includes the existing CRLF handling for headers, so the output doesn't end up with `\r\r\n`. The header is kept for write-back and for `--diff`/`--color-diff` output.

title: blackd: keep the skipped first line inside the returned diff
body:
### Description

`blackd` computes the response patch in `format_code()`, but the first line that was
skipped for `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` was re-attached to the formatted output afterwards
in `handle()`. With `X-Diff: true` and `X-Skip-Source-First-Line: true` combined, the
response body was therefore a raw source line pasted in front of a unified diff of only
the remaining text:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
In	2026-10-21 12:00:00.000000+00:00
Out	2026-10-21 12:00:00.100000+00:00
@@ -1 +1 @@
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

That is not a valid patch — the leading `#!/usr/bin/env python` is neither a diff header
nor a hunk body, so `patch`/`git apply` reject it, and the returned line numbers describe
the request with its first line removed.

Moving the `header` into `format_code()` and restoring it before `only_diff` is handled
puts the skipped line into both sides of the diff, so it shows up as context and the hunks
describe the whole request body:

```
--- [Deterministic header]
+++ [Deterministic header]
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env python
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

Behaviour for the existing combinations is unchanged: `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` without
`X-Diff` still returns the skipped line followed by the formatted source (the assertion in
`test_blackd_skip_first_source_line` still passes), and `X-Diff` alone is untouched since
`header` is then the empty string. `req_str = header + req_str` in `handle()` was dead
code — the local rebinding was never read again — so it is removed along with the
post-hoc concatenation.

No existing issue; I found this while reading the handler. The changelog entry uses the
number this PR is expected to get (#5573); happy to adjust if it lands differently.

title: Parse unpacking in a generator passed as the only call argument (PEP 798)
body:
### Description

PEP 798 support covers `[*x for x in y]`, `(*x for x in y)` and the set and dict forms, but `sum(*x for x in y)` still fails with "cannot parse". Python 3.15 accepts a starred generator as the sole call argument, just like `sum(x for x in y)`, while it still rejects `sum(**x for x in y)`.

Changes:

- Grammar: allow an optional `comp_for` after `'*' test` in `argument`. The `'**' test` alternative is unchanged, so the dict unpacking form is still rejected.
- `is_unpacking_comprehension` now also checks `argument` nodes, whose first child is a bare `*` leaf rather than a `star_expr`, so the call form is detected as `UNPACKING_IN_COMPREHENSIONS` and infers Python 3.15.

Long lines split the same way as an unstarred generator argument:

```python
result = some_function_name(
    *very_long_item_name
    for very_long_item_name in some_iterable_name
    if very_long_item_name
)
```

I also ran the formatter under Python 3.15.0b3 without `--fast`, and the AST safety check passes.

Bumps [zizmorcore/zizmor-action](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-action) from 0.6.4 to 0.7.1.
Release notes

Sourced from zizmorcore/zizmor-action's releases.

v0.7.1

zizmor changes

Bug Fixes 🐛🔗

  • Fixed a regression in 1.31.0 where some ignore comments/configurations would no longer apply to the dangerous-triggers audit

action changes

The default version of zizmor is now 1.31.1.

What's Changed

  • Sync zizmor versions by @​github-actions[bot] in zizmorcore/zizmor-action#178

Full Changelog: https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-action/compare/v0.7.0...v0.7.1

v0.7.0

Sponsorship is appreciated!

zizmor notes

Enhancements 🌱🔗

  • The typosquat-uses audit now supports pre-commit config inputs (#2437)

  • The self-hosted-runner audit is now significantly more precise (#2350)

    Many thanks to @​ubiratansoares for proposing and implementing this enhancement!

  • The dangerous-triggers audit now considers the issue_comment trigger fundamentally dangerous (#2396)

  • zizmor is now aware of the image_version workflow trigger (#2397)

  • The dangerous-triggers audit now produces more precise finding/diagnostic spans (#2402)

  • The cache-poisoning audit is now aware of pnpm/setup (#2409)

  • The unpinned-images audit now produces more precise findings when the user's workflow contains an indirect matrix (#2395)

    Many thanks to @​ubiratansoares for proposing and implementing this enhancement!

  • The cache-poisoning audit is now aware of GitHub's new cache-mode: setting, and will skip any findings that would occur when a job has an effective cache-mode: none (#2418)

  • The cache-poisoning audit now flags usages of cache-mode: write and cache-mode: write-only with dangerous triggers, i.e. triggers that give an attacker privileged code execution (#2426)

  • zizmor now uses a tree-sitter grammar for PowerShell that's more precise/capable of capturing more non-trivial PowerShell expressions (#2444)

title: Fix preview generator-parens crash with --skip-magic-trailing-comma
body:
### Description

With `--preview --skip-magic-trailing-comma`, removing redundant parentheses around a generator argument (#5304, #5369) produces unstable formatting:

```console
$ echo 'consume((normalize(record) for record in records_loaded_from_the_database_for_today_and_yesterday),)' > g.py
$ black --preview -C --check g.py
error: cannot format g.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev10+g56a7ee682 on Python (CPython) 3.13.3 produced different code on the second pass of the formatter.
```

The first pass gives `normalize(\n    record\n) for record in ...` and the second gives `normalize(record)\nfor record in ...`. Sweeping the name length, 67 different lengths crash on `main`.

**Cause:** in `visit_power`, the parens in `f((gen))` are made invisible but the atom stays in the tree. The generator's `for` delimiter is therefore one level deeper, inside invisible parens, so `delimiter_split` finds nothing to split on and the right-hand split produces the odd form above. Normally a later internal pass hides this. With `-C`, the comma in `f((gen),)` delays the paren removal by a pass, so the output only settles on the third pass and the stability check fails.

**Fix:** after making the parens invisible, replace the atom with its contents when it contains no comments. `maybe_make_parens_invisible_in_atom` already does the same stripping. Generators with comments inside are left alone, so the expected output in `preview_redundant_generator_parentheses.py` doesn't change. The example now formats as:

```python
consume(
    normalize(record)
    for record in records_loaded_from_the_database_for_today_and_yesterday
)
```

New case file `preview_redundant_generator_parentheses_skip_mtc.py` (flags `--preview --skip-magic-trailing-comma`) fails on `main` and passes with the fix. The same name-length sweep finds 0 crashes. Full test suite: 582 passed, 3 skipped.

AI disclosure: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) found the bug, wrote the fix and test, and drafted this description. I reviewed the change and the test output.

title: Fix preview unpacking-parens crash on multiline targets
body:
### Description

With `--preview`, `remove_redundant_unpacking_parentheses` (#5416) produces unstable formatting when a target's redundant parentheses end up split across lines:

```console
$ echo '(first), second = (third_target_with_a_very_very_very_long_name_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx), d = 1, 2' > u.py
$ black --preview --check u.py
error: cannot format u.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev10+g56a7ee682 on Python (CPython) 3.13.3 produced different code on the second pass of the formatter.
```

The same happens with `del (a), (LONG)` and `[i for (a), (LONG) in c]`, and with `tests/data/cases/preview_unpacking_parens.py` at `-l 10`, `12` or `15`.

**Cause:** `_normalize_unpacking_targets` skips atoms where `_is_atom_multiline(child)` is true. On the first pass, black splits on the now-invisible parens of `(first)` and emits `(\n    first\n)`. On the second pass that atom is multiline, so the parens are kept, and the output differs.

**Fix:** replace the multiline check with `_atom_has_inner_comments()`, so the parens are only kept when there's a comment inside them. That seems to be the case the check was protecting. The example above now formats stably as:

```python
first, second = (
    third_target_with_a_very_very_very_long_name_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx,
    d,
) = (
    1,
    2,
)
```

New case file `preview_unpacking_parens_multiline.py` covers the chained assignment, multiline targets in an assignment and a `for` loop, and a target with a comment inside its parens. It fails on `main` and passes with the fix. Full test suite: 582 passed, 3 skipped.

AI disclosure: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) found the bug, wrote the fix and test, and drafted this description. I reviewed the change and the test output.

title: Split long strings after overloaded operators in string_processing
body:
### Description

Fixes #2334.

Extend the existing unstable `string_processing` feature to split long string
operands after all arithmetic/bitwise operators and augmented assignments,
including operators overloaded by objects such as `pathlib.Path`.

```python
# Before: --preview --enable-unstable-feature string_processing -l 20
x /= "directory subdirectory file.txt"

# After, with the same input and flags
x /= (
    "directory"
    " subdirectory"
    " file.txt"
)
```

- Reuse the existing operator sets for string splitting and assignment width
  calculations, and recognize terminal or middle string operands in binary expressions.
- Do not treat a following `%` operation as part of that operand: wrapping
  `x % STRING % y` as `x % (STRING % y)` would change associativity.
- Preserve the operand in the tree until operator whitespace has been calculated,
  so `**` keeps the correct spacing when the string is wrapped.

The transformer remains behind the existing **unstable** string-processing flag;
this does not enable string processing in stable or ordinary `--preview` mode.
The new tests cover all 13 binary operators, all 13 augmented assignments
(including width-boundary cases), and six precedence regressions. A formatting
fixture and Future Style documentation are included.

Enclosing calls/collections are split first to preserve existing formatting.

The existing data fixtures retain all 45 original unstable inputs and 26 stable
inputs. The six formerly unchanged middle-operand expectations now require wrapping;

That gives 52 unstable and 32 stable input cases. No function-based tests were added.

title: Make the documented -v example match what black actually prints
body:
### Description

The `-v`/`--verbose` example in `docs/usage_and_configuration/the_basics.md` shows two lines that don't match what the CLI actually prints:

1. `Using configuration from /tmp/pyproject.toml.` — when the config file is auto-discovered (no `--config` passed, which is the case in the shown command `black src/ -v`), `main` prints `Using configuration from project root.` (`src/black/__init__.py:660-664`, the `ParameterSource.DEFAULT` branch). The message that names the file is spelled `Using configuration in '<path>'.` and only appears when `--config` is passed explicitly. So the shown line can never be printed by the shown command.
2. The summary line ends without a period. `get_summary_message` always appends a final `"."` (`src/black/report.py:122`), and the other summary examples in the same file already end with a period (e.g. line 472).

Two one-token fixes inside the existing fenced block; no prose changes.

title: Do not translate the newline twice when writing to stdout
body:
## What

When the input uses CRLF line endings and does not end with a newline, `--stdin` output can end in
`\r\r\n` instead of `\r\n`:

```python
# src/black/__init__.py, _write_to_stdout() path
if dst and dst[-1] != "\n" and dst[-1] != "\r":
    dst += newline        # newline is already "\r\n" here
```

`_write_to_stdout()` translates `\n` to `newline` itself when it writes, so appending `newline`
produces `\r` + translated `\r\n`. The same fixup therefore applies the platform newline twice.

Reproduced on Windows with `black --ipynb -` fed a notebook whose content uses CRLF and has no
trailing newline: the output ends `}\r\r\n`; feeding that output back in is not idempotent. The
error-reporting path has the same shape (`... \r\r\n` at the end of an echoed source line).

## The change

Append a bare `"\n"` instead of `newline`, matching what `__init__.py:1085` already does for the
other write-back branch. One line, no behaviour change on LF input, no change to the formatted code.

## Verification

A 7-assertion byte-level repro (`%TEMP%` venv, `python -m black`):

- before: 3/7 pass — `\r\r\n` in both paths, and the output is not idempotent;
- after: 7/7 pass, and `--ipynb -` output is byte-identical to the input plus a single `\r\n`.

Two regression tests were added: one in `tests/test_black.py` (runs on every CI job) and one in
`tests/test_ipynb.py` (the jupyter-gated file). Neighbouring suites:
`pytest tests/test_black.py tests/test_ipynb.py tests/test_ranges.py tests/test_format.py
tests/test_tokenize.py tests/test_trans.py` → 599 passed, 5 skipped, 2 failed; the 2 failures are
pre-existing Windows-only `--color` tests that fail identically on the unmodified tree.

The `CHANGES.md` entry cites this PR number, as the changelog workflow requires.

title: Don't strip parens that protect merged strings in function argument defaults
body:
### Description

Fixes #3497.

With the string processing feature (`--enable-unstable-feature string_processing`), an implicitly concatenated string used as a function argument default value is merged by `StringMerger`, which registers custom split points for the merged group. If the source wrapped the concatenation in parentheses, `StringParenStripper` then removed them as redundant — but they were not: after stripping, the merged group is glued to the `name=` prefix, `StringSplitter` only matches lines that start with a string (or a string operator), and no brackets are left to split. The result is a line longer than the line length limit:

```python
def open_file_from_long_file_path(
    file_path="some/really/long/file/path/because/it/has/filehash/as/part/of/path/460e96a3b663f41a8412527424278bc60eb208ec5be1f5943e5dff2fe428a2da/file.txt",
):
    pass
```

`StringParenStripper` now keeps the parentheses when stripping them would leave an already-too-long line whose merged string group is still glued to an `=` prefix: the parens are the only way for the layout to split the group at its custom breakpoints. After the fix the example above is formatted as:

```python
def open_file_from_long_file_path(
    file_path=(
        "some/really/long/file/path/because/it/has/filehash/as/part/of/path/"
        "460e96a3b663f41a8412527424278bc60eb208ec5be1f5943e5dff2fe428a2da/"
        "file.txt"
    ),
):
    pass
```

Contexts that can still be split after stripping are unaffected (e.g. call arguments, or strings following a comparison operator such as `assert x == (...)`).

The change is confined to the string processing feature: `StringParenStripper` is only wired into transformer chains when that feature is enabled, so stable and plain preview formatting are unchanged.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (the affected code only runs for the `--unstable` string processing feature)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary? (under "Preview style")
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary? (regression case in `preview_long_strings__regression.py`; it fails without the fix)
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (bug fix only — no documentation update needed)

title: Put each string literal of an implicit concatenation on its own line in preview style
body:
### Description

Implements the change welcomed in #1540, scoped to what the issue actually asks for: in preview style, a line break is inserted after each string literal of an implicit concatenation that ends with a newline, instead of joining everything onto a single line. So the original example from the issue now stays:

```python
ValueError(
    "Invalid input:\n"
    f" * x={x}\n"
    f" * y={y}\n"
    f" * z={z}"
)
```

while a concatenation whose literals don't end in newlines (`f("Data: " f"{foo: <4} | " ...)`) keeps today's joining behavior. Nested brackets cascade (the enclosing call explodes first, then the literals split), and magic trailing commas keep working.

Scope choices worth flagging: a concatenation wrapped in its own parentheses - visible or the invisible ones black puts around assignment right-hand sides and dict values - is treated as a single atom and left alone, so `x = "a\n" "b"` and `d = {"key": "x\n" "y"}` are unchanged. That keeps this PR to "the issue as originally written" without the paren-adding can of worms; happy to take those cases in a follow-up if wanted. The unstable `string_processing` pipeline is untouched.

On the impact question from the thread: diffing this branch against current main preview over pip, pygments, sphinx, the geti backend and sglang/srt, the files that newly differ are 0, 2 (test files), 4 (LaTeX builders/tests), 0 and 0 respectively, so the blast radius looks small.

body:
<!-- Hello! Thanks for submitting a PR. To help make things go a bit smoother

### Description

`docs/faq.md:101` answers *"Can I run Black with PyPy?"* with:

> Yes, there is support for PyPy 3.8 and higher.

Black cannot be installed on a 3.8 interpreter, so that floor is no longer
true: `pyproject.toml:37` sets `requires-python = ">=3.10"`. The FAQ contradicts
itself two sections earlier — `docs/faq.md:88-89` records that "Runtime support

version 24.10.0, and for 3.9 in version 25.12.0."

fix is to raise the number rather than delete the answer. What CI actually runs

exclusion at `:45`), via the `ci-pypy3` environment
(`tox.ini:28`, invoked at `.github/workflows/test.yml:69`). `>=3.10` is the
lowest version the package metadata allows, so the answer becomes:

> Yes, there is support for PyPy 3.10 and higher.

I chose to state the metadata floor rather than "3.11" (the version CI

title: concurrency: count cancelled tasks as failures (fixes #5541)
body:
## Bug (fixes #5541)

`schedule_formatting` collects cancelled tasks into a `cancelled` list and gathers them for cleanup, but never counts them anywhere. When `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` arrives mid-run on a multi-file invocation, the signal handler cancels every pending task; only the files that already finished are reported. `Report.failure_count` stays at `0`, `return_code` stays at `0`, and the summary prints `All done` — so

```sh
black --check . && git push
```

keeps going after an interrupted check even though files were never examined. Reproduces back to `22.1.0`.

## Fix

Record each cancelled task's source along with the task, and after the `gather` call `report.failed(src, ...)` once per cancelled source. `failure_count` then matches the number of files that never got checked, `return_code` becomes non-zero (`123`), and the summary reports the failures instead of claiming success.

Diff is ~12 lines in `src/black/concurrency.py`; already-finished results are still reported normally in the loop above.

## Tests

New regression test `test_cancelled_tasks_count_as_failures` in `tests/test_schedule_formatting.py`:
- Hooks `asyncio.ensure_future` so every scheduled task is cancelled immediately after creation, mirroring what the real signal handler does.
- Asserts `failure_count == len(sources)`, `change_count == 0`, `same_count == 0`, and `return_code != 0`.
- Verified it fails without the patch (`failure_count == 0`) and passes with it.
- The two existing `schedule_formatting` tests (success path and per-file failure path) still pass.

title: Fix headers swallowed by comment-only fmt: off blocks
body:
<!-- Hello! Thanks for submitting a PR. To help make things go a bit smoother
     we would appreciate that you go through this template. -->

### Description

A `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` block that only holds comments has no newline at the
end. When the next line is a compound statement header with `# fmt: skip`, Black
puts the header on the same line as `# fmt: on`, so it turns into part of the
comment.

Input:

```python
def setup():
    connect()


# fmt: off
# fmt: on
if DEBUG :  # fmt: skip
    enable_tracing()
```

`black --fast` exits with 0 and writes:

```python
def setup():
    connect()


    # fmt: off
# fmt: onif DEBUG :  # fmt: skip
    enable_tracing()
```

The `if` is gone and `enable_tracing()` is now inside `setup()`. Without `--fast`,
Black fails with an internal error instead. The same thing happens with
`--line-ranges` when the header is outside the selected lines, even without
`# fmt: skip`.

The `# fmt: skip` case started in 26.10.0 with #5401. The `--line-ranges` case is
older, it also happens on 26.5.1.

The fix adds the missing newline in the two places that join this block with the
code after it, one in `comments.py` and one in `ranges.py`. I added tests for `if`,
`elif`, `else`, `while`, `with`, `finally`, `def`, `class` and `case` headers.

#5525 fixes a different spot in `ranges.py` for the same kind of block (simple
statements and decorators). The two PRs don't overlap.

title: Avoid adding redundant parentheses around unsplittable strings (#3466)
body:
### Description

Fixes #3466.

#### Background
When preview string processing is enabled, `StringParenWrapper` determines whether an argument or collection element is an atom string that should be parenthesized by calling `_prefer_paren_wrap_match`. Previously, it only checked `not any(char == " " for char in LL[0].value)`.

This caused Black to wrap strings in redundant parentheses `( ... )` when the string itself could not actually be split:
1. f-strings where spaces only exist within interpolation expressions `{ ... }` (e.g., `{ 1 }`).
2. Regular strings where spaces only exist inside `\N{...}` named unicode escapes.
3. Strings where spaces are only present within `MIN_SUBSTR_SIZE` (< 6 characters) of the string boundaries.

#### Summary of Changes
- Moved `_iter_nameescape_slices`, `_iter_fexpr_slices`, `_get_illegal_split_indices`, and `MIN_SUBSTR_SIZE` to `BaseStringSplitter`.
- Added `_is_valid_split_index()` and `can_be_split()` methods to `BaseStringSplitter` (reused by `StringSplitter. passes_all_checks`).
- Updated `_prefer_paren_wrap_match` to return `None` when `not self.can_be_split(LL[0].value) and not self. has_custom_splits(LL[0].value) and not line.comments`.
- Added unit tests for `can_be_split()` in `tests/test_trans.py`.
- Added integration test cases in `tests/data/cases/preview_long_strings__edge_case.py`.
- Updated `CHANGES.md`.

title: Remove redundant parentheses around operands in comparison expressions (#2581)
body:
## Summary

Closes #2581.

Under `--preview`, Black now removes redundant parentheses around operands in comparison expressions (e.g. `a == ("str")` -> `a == "str"`, `assert (foo()) == (bar())` -> `assert foo() == bar()`), avoiding surprising unbalanced line breaks.

### Details & Safety Boundaries
- Added the `remove_redundant_comparison_parentheses` preview feature.
- Outer parentheses around leaves (literals, names), attribute access, calls, subscripts, container literals (`[1, 2]`, `{"a": 1}`, `{1, 2}`), unary factors (`-1`, `~x`), and redundant nested parens (`((x))`) are removed.
- Preserves parentheses for:
  - Lower or equal precedence operations (`and`, `or`, `not`, ternaries, lambdas, walrus expressions `:=`, chained comparisons, `yield`)
  - Tuples (`(1, 2)`, `(1,)`, `()`)
  - Generators (`(x for x in y)`)
  - Binary operations (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`, `**`)
  - Operands with comments

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after an opening bracket followed by more code
body:
### Description

Since 26.10.0, a `# fmt: skip` on an opening bracket crashes Black when more code follows the closing bracket on the same line:

```python
x = [  # fmt: skip
    1, 2] + [3]
```

```
error: cannot format file.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.1 on Python (CPython) 3.14.7 produced invalid code:
cannot parse: 3:0:     + [
```

The same happens for `{...} | {...}`, `(...) + 2`, `[...].copy()`, `if [...] == [2]:` and `return [...] + [2]`. 26.5.1 formats all of these.

Bisects to #5144: `_force_standalone_comment_split` starts a new line after every standalone comment, but the comment created by `# fmt: skip` here holds code that ends at the closing bracket, not in a comment, so `+ [3]` lands on its own line. #5405 fixed the same split for a compound header's `:` (#5402); this covers the rest of the line.

The fix keeps the following leaves on the same line when the standalone comment was converted from `# fmt: skip` / `# fmt: off` and its last line has no `#`. If there is any `#` on that line (for example, a trailing `# fmt: skip`), the split stays as before. The output is the same as 26.5.1's.

This is different from #5522, which handles `# fmt: skip` after a closing bracket. I checked that its patch doesn't fix these inputs.

AI disclosure: this was found with a comment-injection fuzzer, bisected and fixed with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5). The new test case fails before the change and passes after; the full test suite has the same results before and after.

title: Fix lambda turned into a tuple by a comment in its default
body:
<!-- Hello! Thanks for submitting a PR. To help make things go a bit smoother

### Description

<!-- Good things to put here include: reasoning for the change (please link
