     story :) -->

Black can turn a lambda into a tuple when a lambda default has a comment on its own line
and the lambda is inside parentheses with a comment after the opening bracket:

```python
handler = (  # comment
    lambda x=(
        # comment
        1,
    ): x
)
```

On 26.10.1 Black adds a comma after the lambda (`): x,`), so `handler` becomes a tuple.
In safe mode this fails with "produced code that is not equivalent to the source". With
`--fast` (or blackd in fast mode) the changed code is written to the file.

The comment splits the line in the middle of the default's brackets. The rest of the line
(`1,): x`) then goes to `delimiter_split`, which treats the comma inside the default as a
top level comma and adds a trailing comma at the end of the line. Now `delimiter_split`
doesn't add a trailing comma when the line closes a bracket that was opened on an earlier
line.

The same split also caused the opposite problem with `--skip-magic-trailing-comma`: the
required comma in a one-element subscript like `a[1,]` was removed. #5246 fixed this for
tuples, so I added a subscript check next to the tuple check.

Already formatted code doesn't change.

Fixes #5536. Related: #4640, #4296, #5241.

title: Echo force-excluded stdin input unchanged
body:
### Description

Fixes #5529.

When a file passed through stdin matches `--force-exclude`, Black prints the input back as it is (added in #4610). It does this with `sys.stdout.write(sys.stdin.read())`. That goes through the text streams, so the output is not always the same as the input:

- On Windows, LF line endings come back as CRLF.
- If the file is not UTF-8 and stdin decodes strictly, Black crashes with `UnicodeDecodeError`.
- With `--check` or `--diff`, the whole file is printed to stdout.

This PR copies the bytes from stdin to stdout without changing them, and only when Black would write the result back. With `--check` or `--diff` nothing is printed, the same as for a file that needs no changes.

The new test also fails without the fix on Linux, because the test runner's stdin and stdout change line endings too.

title: Normalize hex codes in unicode escape sequences in f-strings (#4523)
body:
Closes #4523

### Summary
When PR #4401 prevented quotes from normalizing inside f-strings containing backslashes (to avoid syntax errors like `f"{'\''}"` turning into `f"{'''}"`), it bypassed `visit_STRING`, completely suppressing normalize_unicode_escape_sequences() for f-strings.

This PR introduces normalize_fstring_unicode_escape_sequences() to safely normalize hex codes in unicode escape sequences (e.g. `\xFF` -> `\xff`, `\u00A0` -> `\u00a0`, `\N{...}` -> uppercase) within f-strings and t-strings while preserving AST equivalence:
- **Raw f-strings:** Skips template parts when the f-string prefix contains `r`/`R` (e.g. `rf"..."`).
- **Raw string literals in replacement fields:** Preserves expressions like `f"{r'\xFF'}"` without mutating escaped characters, preventing runtime value changes and `ASTSafetyError`.
- **Debug f-strings:** Leaves expressions preceding `=` intact (e.g. `f"{'\xFF'=}"`) since Python prints the literal source representation before `=` at runtime.
- **Nested templates:** Recursively handles nested f-strings and t-strings.

### Test Plan
- Added cases to pep_701.py covering raw f-strings, nested f-strings, debug f-strings (`=`), raw string literals in fields, `\N{...}`, `\u...`, and `\U...`.
- Added test case to format_unicode_escape_seq.py.
- Verified full test suite (`pytest`) and linters (`flake8`, `black --check`).

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a multi-line call in brackets
body:
### Description

`# fmt: skip` after the closing bracket of a multi-line call or subscript crashes Black when that element isn't the last one in a collection or argument list:

```python
x = {
    "a": 1,
    "b": f(
        a  ,  b
    ),  # fmt: skip
    "c": 2,
}
```

fails with "Unable to match a closing bracket to the following opening bracket: }". Inside a call's arguments it fails with "produced invalid code" instead.

When collecting the nodes on the skipped line, a closing bracket is already widened to its whole parenthesized expression (#4855), but not to a call or subscript. So only `)` and `,` were hidden while the matching `(` stayed in the tree. This now also widens the bracket to the call or subscript trailer, so just that element is left as is and the rest of the collection is still formatted.

title: Fix string_processing crash on strings in collections at small line lengths
body:
### Description

Fixes #3424.

With the unstable `string_processing` feature, Black wraps list, tuple and set elements in parens even when the wrapped line is still over the line length and can't be split there. At line length 8, two of the three elements of the issue's list still get wrapped that way. When the elements also carry comments, as below, Black fails with "produced different code on the second pass" at line lengths 1 to 8. So does a tuple or a set, and the list nested 20 deep at the default line length.

```python
l3 = [
    "I have",  # c
    "trailing comma",  # c
    "so I should be braked",
]
```

In the crash, `StringSplitter` gives up on a wrapped string because the line is too deep to split, after it has already taken the string out of the tree. The closing paren then lands one slot off, and the next element is split bare on the first pass and wrapped on the second.

`StringParenWrapper` now skips the wrap when the new line would still be too long and can't be split, which Black already does for strings without spaces. The elements stay as written, so the line that set off the crash is never created.

The new test case covers the issue's list, tuple and set and the commented list. It fails on main and passes with this change. I also formatted all test case inputs and 1,486 real files with main and this branch. Output at the default line length is identical in every mode. Under `--unstable` at small line lengths, 16 test case results and 2 files that crash on main now format, and every other difference is these parens being left off, plus one tuple where main split a string bare.

title: Remove parentheses around simple top-level expressions (#4231)
body:
### Description

Closes #4231.

Currently, redundant parentheses around simple top-level expressions (`simple_stmt`) are preserved even with `--preview` or `--unstable`:
    
    (x)
    (1)
    (yield 42)
    ([])
    ({})
    (a + b)

This PR introduces the Preview.remove_redundant_top_level_parentheses preview style feature to remove redundant parentheses around simple top-level expressions:

    x
    1
    yield 42
    []
    {}
    a + b

Key behaviors and safety considerations:

• Walrus assignments: Preserves statement-level parentheses around (x := 1) since unparenthesized assignment expressions at the statement level are invalid Python syntax.
• Tuples and generator expressions: Standard delimiter priorities keep tuples ((), (x,), (a, b)) and generator expressions ((x for x in y)) parenthesized at statement level.
• Implicit string concatenation: Statements with implicitly concatenated strings (e.g. ("a" "b")) retain parentheses so multiline splits do not separate into distinct string statements.
• Yield expressions: Parens around (yield 42) and (yield) at statement level are removed, while expressions in argument positions like f((yield 42)) retain their mandatory parentheses.
• Comments and multiline splits: Standalone comments inside parentheses retain their enclosing brackets, and expressions exceeding the line length automatically convert invisible parens into visible brackets when splitting lines.

title: Avoid OSError: AF_UNIX path too long for multiprocessing manager when running --diff (#2105)
body:
### Description
Fixes #2105.

#### Problem
When `black --diff` (or `--color`) is run on multiple files in environments with a long temporary directory path (very common in macOS and Linux CI environments like GitHub Actions runners or container builds), Black crashes with:
    ```text
    Process SyncManager-1:
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      ...
      File ".../multiprocessing/connection.py", line 596, in __init__
        self._socket.bind(address)
    OSError: AF_UNIX path too long

Aborted!

This occurs because black.concurrency.schedule_formatting instantiates multiprocessing.Manager() to create a lock for synchronizing diff output to stdout. On POSIX systems, SyncManager creates a Unix domain socket inside tempfile.gettempdir(). POSIX systems enforce a strict kernel limit for sockaddr_un.sun_path (104 bytes on macOS/BSD, 108 bytes on Linux). When $TMPDIR exceeds ~68 characters, the generated socket path (<tempdir>/pymp-XXXXXXXX/listener-YYYYYYYY) overflows the buffer and bind() fails.

#### Solution

1. Redirect to safe temporary directory: Added _safe_multiprocessing_tempdir() and _get_safe_tempdir() in black.concurrency. On POSIX systems, if tempfile.gettempdir() exceeds the safe length threshold for Unix domain sockets, it temporarily points TMPDIR and tempfile.tempdir to a short, standard, writable directory (e.g. /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm) during Manager() startup, and restores the original value afterwards.
2. Graceful fallback: Wrapped Manager() creation in a try ... except (OSError, EOFError): block to fall back to lock = None so Black proceeds with formatting and generating diffs rather than crashing if multiprocessing socket creation fails.
3. Tests: Added unit tests verifying short paths are untouched, long paths are redirected to safe short paths and restored, graceful fallback on manager startup errors, and end-to-end CLI execution with long TMPDIR.

title: Handle PEP 695 type parameter whitespace in whitespace()
body:
`visit_typeparams`, `visit_typevartuple`, and `visit_paramspec` removed the space after `[`, `*`, and `**` by clearing the leaf prefix after `visit_default` had appended it. That only works for the lines built by `LineGenerator`: whenever a transformer rebuilds a line through `append_leaves` without `preformatted=True`, `whitespace()` runs again and reinstates the space. The unstable `string_processing` feature does exactly that when it splits a string inside a type parameter default, producing

```python
def f[
    * Ts = Set[
        "..."
        " ..."
    ]
]():
```

Teach `whitespace()` the three cases directly, which is where every other bracket and vararg rule lives, and drop the post-hoc prefix fixups. Stable output is unchanged; the existing `type_params.py` and `type_param_defaults.py` cases cover the simple forms, and the new case covers the rebuilt-line path.

title: Keep walrus parentheses in set literals for Python 3.9 and older targets
body:
### Description

When the target versions include Python 3.9 or older, Black removes the parentheses
around a walrus that is the only item in a set:

```python
# input, works on Python 3.8
x = {(y := 1)}

# output with `black -t py38`
x = {y := 1}
```

Python 3.8 and 3.9.0 can't parse the output, so the file fails with a `SyntaxError`. Black still
exits with 0, and the safety check doesn't catch it because Black itself runs on 3.10 or
newer. The same happens with `requires-python = ">=3.8"` and with auto-detection, since
a walrus makes Black infer 3.8 as the lowest target.

This comes from removing parentheses around a lone list or set item (#4312). A walrus
without parentheses in a set is only valid from Python 3.10 (3.9.1 added it, but 3.9.0
can't parse it).

The fix adds a feature for 3.10 and newer and keeps the parentheses when the targets
include 3.9 or older. Extra parentheses are still removed, so `{((y := 1))}` becomes
`{(y := 1)}`. For 3.10+ targets the output doesn't change, and code that Black already
formatted is left alone, so I think this is fine under the stability policy.

title: Enable cache when running with --diff (#1145)
body:
## Summary
Resolves #1145.

Running `black --diff` previously bypassed the cache entirely, re-formatting all files across the repository even when they were already well-formatted and cached. This caused large performance penalties on big projects where `black --check .` would run in sub-second time using cache, but `black --diff .` would take minutes.

This PR enables reading and writing the per-user cache for `WriteBack.DIFF` and `WriteBack.COLOR_DIFF`:
- If a file is cached and unmodified on disk, it is recognized as `Changed.CACHED` and skipped (producing 0 diff).
- If a file is formatted during `--diff` and found to have no changes (`Changed.NO`), it is recorded in the cache as well formatted.
- If a file produces diffs (`Changed.YES`), it is not cached (so subsequent runs continue to show the diff until reformatted).

## Changes
- In `src/black/__init__.py`: removed exclusion of `DIFF` and `COLOR_DIFF` from checking `cache.is_changed`, and allowed writing to cache when `changed is Changed.NO`.
- In `src/black/concurrency.py`: removed exclusion of `DIFF` and `COLOR_DIFF` from `cache.filtered_cached(sources)` and added cache recording for files with `Changed.NO`.
- In `docs/usage_and_configuration/file_collection_and_discovery.md`: removed the outdated note stating `--diff` disables the cache.
- In `CHANGES.md`: documented under `### Configuration`.
- In `tests/test_black.py`: added comprehensive unit tests for single-file and multi-file cache behavior with `--diff` (both colored and non-colored).

## Test Plan
- `pytest tests/test_black.py -k "cache"` passes (35 tests).
- Full test suite passes: `557 passed, 8 skipped`.
- `black --check` and `flake8` pass cleanly.

title: Avoid splitting trailers when earlier bracket split exceeds length due to comments (#3681)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #3681.

When a line containing an opening parenthesis/bracket is split, but the resulting head line exceeds `line_length` solely  because of a trailing comment (e.g. `# type: ignore`), `right_hand_split_with_omits` previously rejected the split and fell back to `first_lines` (no omits). This caused unrelated trailing indexing/subscripts (such as `[0]`) on later lines to be exploded across multiple lines, even though the head line could not be shortened by splitting them and ended up exceeding the limt regardless.

## Changes

- Updated `_over_length_only_due_to_bracket_comment` in `src/black/linegen.py` to allow any opening bracket in `OPENING_BRACKETS` (`(`, `[`, `{`) when evaluating omit candidates in `right_hand_split_with_omits`.
- Retained the subscript-specific check (`token.LSQB`) for `run_transformer` to preserve behavior for assignments and prevent comment-migration oscillations.
- Added regression tests in `tests/data/cases/comment_on_opening_bracket.py`.
- Added a changelog entry to `CHANGES.md`.

## Test Plan

- `pytest tests/test_format.py -k "comment_on_opening_bracket"`
- Full pytest test suite (`pytest tests/`) passes cleanly.
- `flake8`, `mypy`, and `black --check` all pass.

title: Skip UTF-8 BOM when reading .gitignore
body:
### Description

If a .gitignore starts with a UTF-8 BOM, Black ignores the first
pattern in it. Git skips the BOM so the pattern still works there,
but Black reads it as part of the pattern, so it never matches. So
Black ends up formatting files that git ignores.

Some editors and tools on Windows save files with a BOM.

To reproduce:

```sh
mkdir demo && cd demo && git init
mkdir generated
printf '\xef\xbb\xbfgenerated/\n' > .gitignore
printf 'x   =   1\n' > generated/models.py
git check-ignore generated/models.py  # git says it is ignored
black --check .  # black wants to reformat generated/models.py
```

The fix opens .gitignore with utf-8-sig instead of utf-8. That drops
the BOM if there is one and reads normal UTF-8 files the same as
before. I added a test with a BOM in both a root and a nested
.gitignore.

title: Fix #3679: Remove redundant parentheses in getitem/indexing operators
body:
Fixes #3679

**Description**
This PR introduces the `remove_redundant_subscript_parentheses` preview style to automatically remove redundant parentheses in `getitem` and indexing operators.

Specifically, it formats expressions like:
    ```python
        [][(1)] -> [][1]
        a[(1, 2)] -> a[1, 2]

However, it correctly preserves parentheses when they are semantically required or affect the AST structure, such as:

• Empty tuples: a[()]
• Generators: a[(x for x in y)]
• Inner trailing commas: a[(1,)] (stays as a[1,])

Testing

• Added the preview_redundant_subscript_parentheses.py test case.
• Passed all formatting tests locally using pytest.

title: Fix module docstring last_line_length when docstring ends with newline
body:
When formatting a multiline docstring whose closing triple quotes are
preceded by a newline and trailing spaces (e.g. a module docstring where
indent is empty), fix_multiline_docstring strips the trailing spaces so
docstring ends with '\n'. Because splitlines() does not return a trailing
empty element when a string ends with '\n', len(lines[-1]) measured the
length of the preceding content line rather than the empty last line.
When that preceding line was within 3 characters of line_length, we
appended an extra '\n' before the closing quotes, leaving a trailing
blank line inside the docstring.

Treat last_line_length as 0 when docstring.endswith('\n').

title: Preserve blank lines after imports with --line-ranges
body:
When formatting with --line-ranges, EmptyLineTracker._maybe_empty_lines
treated unselected non-import lines after a formatted import as regular
formatted lines and collapsed existing multiple blank lines down to 1
(or forced 2 blank lines before an unselected class in preview mode).
Conversely, when the import line itself was unselected and the following
statement was formatted, it failed to ensure at least 1 blank line after
the import block.

Update _maybe_empty_lines to:
- Only force 2 blank lines before fmt_pass_converted classes when they
  were converted by # fmt: off (line_ranges_selected is None), not
  --line-ranges.
- Preserve existing blank lines before any fmt_pass_converted line after
  an import.
- Ensure at least 1 blank line after an unselected import line when the
  following line is formatted (excluding unselected standalone comments
  and pairs of unselected lines).

title: Keep the parentheses around a right-hand side when a dict value's parentheses are made invisible
body:
### Description

Fixes #5488.

With `--preview`, this assignment loses the parentheses around its right-hand side and the first line grows to 96 characters:

```python
self.a_long_class_attribute_to_use = A_LONG_TEMPLATE_CONSTANT_NAME_HERE.safe_substitute(
    {
        "n": (
            "long text that breaks the ternary" if A_LONG_CONSTANT_NAME else ""
        ),
    },
)
```

Stable style keeps the parentheses because of the second opinion in `run_transformer`: when the first line of a right-hand split is still too long, it retries with `FORCE_OPTIONAL_PARENTHESES` and takes that result if every line fits. The retry is skipped when one of the line's invisible parens has turned visible, because that means the split already used them.

`wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens` makes the dict value's own parens invisible, so they sit in the same `bracket_tracker.invisible` list as the line's optional parens. Splitting the sub-line for the dict value makes them visible again, the guard reads that as "the optional parens were used", and the retry never runs. The line's own optional parens are still invisible at that point.

Under `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens`, the guard now looks only at the line's top-level invisible parens (`bracket_depth == 0`). The depths are read before the transform runs, because the sub-line splits re-mark the same leaves. Stable style takes the same code path as before, since the filter only applies with the preview feature on. The output now matches stable's shape:

```python
self.a_long_class_attribute_to_use = (
    A_LONG_TEMPLATE_CONSTANT_NAME_HERE.safe_substitute(
        {
            "n": (
                "long text that breaks the ternary" if A_LONG_CONSTANT_NAME else ""
            ),
        },
    )
)
```

The existing `Random.func` case in `preview_long_dict_values.py` had the same bug: its expected output had a 90-character first line. It now wraps the right-hand side and fits in 88, so this PR updates that expectation.

Verification:

- The new case in `preview_long_dict_values.py` fails on `main` and passes with the fix. It lands in its own commit before the fix.
- The full test suite passes: 551 passed, 3 skipped. That includes `preview_long_strings__regression`, which the length-based approach discussed in the issue broke.
- `--preview` output is byte-identical before and after the change across 2,268 files (installed site-packages, `celery`, `agno`, `mempalace`).
- A second review ran 57 extra inputs (chained, annotated and augmented assignments, `return`, `del`, `for`, `with`, lambdas, comments, `type: ignore`) at line lengths 1, 40, 60, 88 and 120 in preview and unstable. None crashed, all were stable on a second pass, and none came out wider than on `main`.
- pre-commit (isort, flake8, mypy, prettier) passes.

AI disclosure: an AI agent (Claude Code) reproduced the issue, traced the cause, wrote the fix, the test, and this description, and ran the checks above (`pytest tests -n auto`, `pre-commit run`, the corpus comparison against `main`).

title: Parenthesize logical expressions with function calls in preview (#3629)
body:
Fixes #3629.

When a logical expression (`and` / `or`) exceeds the line length and ends with a function call, Black currently splits inside the function call's arguments rather than parenthesizing the whole condition and splitting at the operator.

This PR adds the `parenthesize_logical_operators` preview feature so logical expressions retain their outer parentheses and split cleanly at `and` / `or`.

    ```python
    # Before
    if isinstance(very_long_expression, Sequence) and not isinstance(
        very_long_expression, str
    ):
        ...

    # After (with --preview)
    if (
        isinstance(very_long_expression, Sequence)
        and not isinstance(very_long_expression, str)
    ):
        ...

title: Keep an ignored encoding declaration off the first two lines
body:
### Description

Fixes #5486

If a file starts with blank lines and has an encoding declaration on line 3 or later, Python ignores that declaration. Black removed the blank lines, so the declaration moved to line 1 and Python started using it. The file is still written in its original encoding, so non-ASCII text got decoded differently and the AST check couldn't see it.

As suggested in the review, Black now keeps up to two of the lines before the declaration so it stays ignored, and formats the rest of the file as usual.

- It only keeps the lines when moving the declaration would change how Python decodes the file. A `utf-8` declaration, or one that is already on the first two lines, is formatted the same as before
- The check is at the end of `_format_str_once`, so it covers files, stdin, `-c`, `--line-ranges` and blackd
- A file with an unknown encoding name below line 2 used to fail with `unknown encoding`, it now gets formatted too
- The tests are in `tests/test_black.py` because the test case files strip leading blank lines

title: Fix line-range mapping for a changed start of file
body:
### Description

Part of #4052. Two things kept `--line-ranges` from selecting the right lines when
the first formatting pass rewrote the start of a file.

**1. The lines before the first matching block were recorded as an *unchanged* block**

`_calculate_lines_mappings` marked that region as unchanged even though those lines
have no counterpart on the other side of the diff. A requested range that overlaps
them was therefore mapped by offset instead of being expanded to the changed block,
which is what every other changed block does, and what `adjusted_lines`' docstring
documents.

**2. Lines were compared verbatim**

The first pass re-indents the bodies of the statements it formats, so a line that
only moved within its statement looked like an unrelated change. That turned the
whole file into a single leading block, and mapping the range stayed a no-op. The
comparison ignores leading whitespace now: a line that only moved is still the same
line, and `_LinesMapping` only records where it went.

Together they fix the first case of the issue:

```python
def restrict_to_this_line(arg1,
  arg2,
  arg3):
  print  ( "This should not be formatted." )
  print  ( "This should not be formatted." )
```

With `--line-ranges=1-3`, before: the signature is joined **and** both `print`
statements are formatted, although they were never selected. After: the signature is
joined, and the `print` statements keep the indentation given by the first pass
without being formatted.

The lines before the first matching block can also disappear entirely, because Black
drops leading empty lines; a selection that only covers them then maps to nothing.
`format_str` passed those empty ranges to the second pass, where an empty `lines`
means "format the whole file", so the file was reformatted in full. The second pass
is now skipped when none of the requested lines survive the first pass.

`tests/test_ranges.py` expected `[(1, 1)]` to be unchanged when the first line is
removed; that line has no counterpart in the modified source, so the case now expects
an empty range. A new parametrized test covers the joined statement at the start of a
file, and end-to-end tests pin both the fixed selection and the "nothing survives"
case.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Follow the stability policy? This changes `--line-ranges` line selection, not Black's formatting style.
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md`? Added under Unreleased `### Stable style`.
- [x] Add / update tests?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? Not needed: `adjusted_lines`' docstring already describes the intended expansion behaviour.

Verification: `pytest tests/test_ranges.py -q -p no:randomly` → 42 passed;
`pytest tests/test_black.py -q -p no:randomly` → 189 passed, 10 subtests passed;
`pytest tests/test_format.py -q -p no:randomly` → 258 passed; the full suite except
`tests/test_blackd.py` (needs the `d` extra) → 505 passed, 3 skipped; `black --check`
on the touched files is clean. A six-case start-of-file battery produces
byte-identical formatted output to `main`; the outputs this PR changes are pinned by
the new end-to-end tests.

_Disclosure: this change was prepared with an AI coding assistant (DeepSeek) under my direction; I reviewed the diff and the commands above before pushing._

title: Don't remove backslash-newlines from raw strings in string_processing
body:
### Description

With the unstable `string_processing` feature, `StringMerger._remove_backslash_line_continuation_chars` removes every `\` + newline sequence from a string leaf. That is correct for regular strings, where the sequence is a line continuation. In a raw string, though, the backslash and the newline are both part of the string's value, so removing them changes the program:

```python
x = r"abc\
def"
```

`black --unstable` (or `--preview --enable-unstable-feature string_processing`) rewrites this to `x = r"abcdef"`. With the safety check on, this fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: ... produced code that is not equivalent to the source". With `--fast`, the value is silently changed. I ran into it while running the unstable style over CPython's `Lib/test`: `Lib/test/test_tokenize.py` (3.13 branch) hits this on `self.check_tokenize(r'Rf"abc\` + newline + `def"', ...)`.

The fix skips string leaves with an `r`/`R` prefix (including `rb`, `rf`, and so on) in that step, the same way triple-quoted strings are already skipped. Regular strings with backslash continuations are still joined as before.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (bug fix in an unstable preview feature)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (not needed)

Test: `tests/data/cases/preview_long_strings__raw_backslash_continuation.py` covers `r`, `rb` and `Rf` strings, plus a regular string that should still be joined. It fails on `main` (the raw strings get joined) and passes with this change. The rest of `pytest tests` passes except `test_expression_diff_with_color` and `test_piping_diff_with_color`, which fail the same way on `main` in my environment. pre-commit (isort, flake8, mypy) passes on the changed files.

title: Fix long notebook magic assignments being wrapped in parentheses
body:
### Description

When a notebook cell has a magic assignment that is longer than the line length, Black
wraps it in parentheses. For example this cell:

```python
installed_packages_in_this_environment = !pip list --format=freeze --disable-pip-version-check
```

becomes:

```python
installed_packages_in_this_environment = (
    !pip list --format=freeze --disable-pip-version-check
)
```

IPython does not accept a magic inside parentheses, so the cell now fails with
`SyntaxError: invalid syntax` when you run it. Black exits with 0, and later runs of
`black --check` also pass because Black skips the broken cell.

The reason is that Black formats the cell with each magic replaced by a placeholder
string. The placeholder can be wrapped like any other string, and the safety check only
sees the placeholder version, so it does not notice the problem.

The fix is in `unmask_cell`. After the magics are put back, it masks the cell again and
checks that IPython still finds the same magics. If it does not, the cell is left
unchanged, the same way Black already skips cells it cannot format safely.

I added tests for a long `!` assignment, a long `%timeit -o` assignment, an indented one,
and a direct test for `unmask_cell`. All of them fail without the fix.

title: Fix GitHub Action crash on dependency-group includes
body:
### Description

With `use_pyproject: true`, the GitHub Action crashes before installing Black when any
`[dependency-groups]` array contains an `{include-group = "..."}` table, which the
[dependency-groups specification](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-groups/)
allows (Black's own `pyproject.toml` uses them):

```toml
[dependency-groups]
dev = [{include-group = "lint"}]
lint = ["black==26.5.1"]
```

```
AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'split'
```

`find_black_version_in_array()` calls `.split(";")` on every entry. Because
`read_version_specifier_from_pyproject()` already scans every dependency group (and then
`project.dependencies` / optional dependencies), an included group is checked on its own,
so the fix only needs to skip non-string entries. Lookup order and version handling are
unchanged; this does not add include resolution or combine specifiers across groups
(deliberately deferred in #4606).

The crash also happens when an unrelated earlier group contains an include and the Black
pin lives in a later group or in `project.dependencies`.

Tests: `tests/test_github_action.py` runs the whole `action/main.py` entrypoint via
`runpy` with `subprocess.run` mocked, and checks the requirement passed to `pip install`
and the formatter invocation. Cases cover includes before/after a pin, a pin inside the
included group, an unrelated include before a `project.dependencies` pin, plain project
pins, extras + markers, and the existing "unpinned" / "missing" error paths. Four of the
eight cases fail with the `AttributeError` above without the fix.

AI assistance (OpenAI Codex / Claude) was used to investigate and prepare this change; the
diff was reviewed before submission.

title: Fix `--line-ranges` crash on `# fmt: skip` before a closing bracket
body:
### Description

With `--line-ranges`, Black turns statements outside the selected ranges into a single `STANDALONE_COMMENT` using `str(node)`. If such a statement has a `# fmt: skip` on the last line before a closing bracket, that comment has already become a nested `STANDALONE_COMMENT` whose value has no trailing newline (the line generator normally adds it). `str(node)` then glues the closing bracket onto the comment's line, so the bracket becomes part of the comment and Black fails on its own output:

```console
$ printf 'x = 1\nv = (\n    a  # fmt: skip\n)\n' > t.py
$ black --line-ranges=1-1 t.py
error: cannot format t.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black ... produced invalid code:
cannot parse: t.py:3:19
    a  # fmt: skip)
                  ^
```

Without `--line-ranges` the same file formats fine, and the lines outside the range should be left alone, so this is an internal error on code the user did not ask to touch.

The fix: when converting an unselected node (`_convert_node_to_standalone_comment` and `_convert_nodes_to_standalone_comment` in `ranges.py`) stringify the node with a helper that ends a nested `STANDALONE_COMMENT` with a newline when it ends in a `# fmt: skip` comment and the next leaf does not already start with a newline. Nothing else changes: a standalone comment that ends in code, such as a header followed by `:` (#5405), is joined as before.

Tests:

- `tests/data/cases/line_ranges_fmt_skip_in_brackets.py`: statements with `# fmt: skip` before a closing bracket (call, tuple, dict, `if` header, `for` iterable) outside the range stay untouched while the selected line is formatted.
- `tests/data/line_ranges_formatted/fmt_skip_in_brackets.py`: the existing line-by-line test runs `--line-ranges` over every line of a formatted file.

Both fail on `main` with `INTERNAL ERROR ... produced invalid code` and pass with the change.

Sibling code paths checked: the other `str(node)` consumer in this feature, `_convert_nodes_to_standalone_comment` (match/suite headers), is changed the same way; `comments.py` already adds newlines for nested standalone comments in its own stringification; `visit_suite` already skips suites that contain a standalone comment. Not in scope: some other `--line-ranges` + `# fmt: off`/`# fmt: skip` combinations still fail (for example an `async for ... in (  # fmt: skip` header outside the range, and `tests/data/cases/fmtonoff5.py`); they have different causes.

Performance: the helper walks the leaves of each converted node once, as `str(node)` did; I saw no consistent difference in a noisy local benchmark (`--line-ranges=1-1` on a 6000-line file).

- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?

title: Avoid quadratic runtime in right_hand_split_with_omits on long lines (#5270)
body:
## Summary
Fixes #5270.
Closes #5275
Closes #5305

Formatting lines containing long chains of consecutive bracket trailers (such as subscript chains `a[0][1]...[160]`) suffered from quadratic runtime due to combinatorial omit trials in `right_hand_split_with_omits`.

### Root Cause
Unlike attribute chains which have dot delimiters and are split cleanly in a single pass by `delimiter_split`, consecutive
  subscript chains `][` have no intermediate delimiters and fall back to `right_hand_split_with_omits`.

`generate_trailers_to_omit` yields bracket pairs from the tail up to `line_length`. In long lines with many small trailers
  (like `[0]...`), Black was performing up to 20 full `right_hand_split` calls per recursion level, only for
  `is_line_short_enough(lines[0])` to fail on every single omit candidate because each candidate split point was still hundreds of
  characters from the start of the line.

### Fix
1. Precompute cumulative prefix lengths for all leaves in `line.leaves` once at the start of `right_hand_split_with_omits`.
2. For each candidate `omit`, inspect the target `opening_bracket` the split would break on. If its prefix length from the start of the line alone exceeds `mode.line_length`, any head line produced by that split is mathematically guaranteed to exceed `line_length`. We safely skip executing `right_hand_split` for that omit.
3. Candidate omits that break on an opening bracket within `mode.line_length` (e.g. `foo(long_args...)[key]`) are retained and evaluated normally.
4. In the final fallback, reuse `first_lines` instead of redundantly re-running `right_hand_split`.
5. Output formatting is 100% invariant across all cases (diff-shades shows 0 changes).

### Benchmark
- $n = 100$ subscripts: ~2.8s -> ~0.35s (~8x speedup, 2,574 RHS calls -> 156 RHS calls)
- $n = 160$ subscripts: ~9.5s -> ~0.35s (~27x speedup)
- $n = 300$ subscripts: >30s -> ~0.95s (~30x speedup)

## Test Plan
- Added `test_subscript_chain_avoids_quadratic_rhs_splits` in `tests/test_black.py` to verify that `right_hand_split` invocations remain linearly bounded ($O(n)$) rather than quadratic ($O(n^2)$).
- Full unit test suite passes.
- All pre-commit checks pass.

title: Avoid unnecessary parens for unbreakable RHS in assignments (#3954)
body:
Fixes #3954                                  
                                                 
### Summary                                  
When an assignment's target contains type
 annotations or brackets (e.g. `attr: str = "long..."`
or `a[0] = "long..."`) and the RHS  
  is an unbreakable expression (like a long      
  string or identifier) that cannot fit within   
  the line length limit even with parentheses,   
  Black previously wrapped the RHS in outer      
  parentheses, creating an inconsistency with    
  standard unannotated assignments (`attr = "long..."`).                                   
                                                 
This happened because 
 `_maybe_split_omitting_optional_parens` found  
  an alternative split on the LHS                
  brackets/invisible parens (`rhs_oop`), rejected
  it via `_prefer_split_rhs_oop_over_rhs`, but   
  then bypassed the validation check that        
  verifies whether the original RHS body can     
  actually be split or fit on one line.          
                                                 
Under `--preview`, Black now recognizes that 
  the alternative split was rejected and falls   
  back to validating the original RHS, leaving   
  unbreakable expressions unparenthesized when   
  wrapping cannot satisfy the line length.

title: Keep trailing type-checker ignore pragmas on the first line of a split
body:
Fixes #3946

## Problem

Ignore pragmas such as `# pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType]` suppress the diagnostics of the expression they trail. When Black splits such a line, the pragma ends up on the last line, after the closing bracket, where it no longer suppresses anything:

```python
# input
asm_client: SecretsManagerClient = boto3.client("secretsmanager")  # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType]

# output (before)
asm_client: SecretsManagerClient = boto3.client(
    "secretsmanager"
)  # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType]
```

## Approach — option one from the review discussion

Reworked per @cobaltt7's feedback: this now only **extends the existing heuristic** that already keeps lines ending with `# type: ignore` unsplit (`contains_unsplittable_type_ignore`) to recognize other type-checker ignore pragmas (`# pyright: ignore[...]`, `# mypy: ignore`, `# ty: ignore`, …). Lines trailing such a pragma stay unsplit, mirroring the `# type: ignore` trade-off. All comment-relocation logic from the earlier revisions is gone.

The pragma pattern requires `ignore` as the last word, optionally followed by a bracketed code list, so prose comments are not mistaken for pragmas; `# type: ignore` keeps its dedicated handling.

## Gating

The behavior is behind the new `unsplittable_ignore_pragmas` preview feature, so stable output is unchanged. Local verification (the workflow runs are still awaiting maintainer approval):

- stable output is byte-identical to `main` on a 256-file corpus sampled from installed packages
- full test suite passes (535 passed, 3 skipped), including the new `preview_unsplittable_ignore_pragmas` cases (issue reproducer, prose-comment non-match, `# type: ignore` regression)

title: Preserve leaf line numbers in append_leaves to prevent pragma line collapse
body:
`append_leaves` constructs `Leaf(old_leaf.type, old_leaf.value)` without copying `old_leaf.lineno`, resetting `lineno` to `0` on all copied leaves.

When `StringMerger` or `StringParenStripper` transforms a multi-line expression that ends with a `# type: ignore` pragma not caught by `StringMerger._validate_msg` (for example, when non-closing-bracket tokens like `,`, `%`, `.format()`, or `+` appear between a merged string group and the pragma-bearing closing bracket), the recursive `transform_line` call invokes `Line.contains_unsplittable_type_ignore`. Because all leaves on the transformed line have `lineno == 0`, `first_line == last_line` (`0 == 0`) evaluates to `True`, causing `transform_line` to treat the multi-line expression as a single-line unsplittable `# type: ignore` and skip all line-splitting transformers (`string_split`, `delimiter_split`, and `rhs`).

Copy `old_leaf.lineno` onto `new_leaf.lineno` in `append_leaves` so transformed lines retain their original source line span, and require `first_line != 0` in `Line.contains_unsplittable_type_ignore` so lines composed entirely of generated leaves are not misclassified as single-line expressions.

title: Keep trailing type-checker ignore pragmas on the first line of a split
body:
### Description

Fixes #3946.

When Black splits a line whose trailing comment is a type-checker ignore pragma (`# pyright: ignore[...]`, `# ty: ignore`, `# mypy: ignore[...]`), the pragma ends up on the last line, after the closing bracket. Type checkers apply these pragmas to the line where the diagnostic originates, which is the first line of the split, so the relocated pragma suppresses nothing.

Following the direction from the issue discussion (a general heuristic rather than a per-tool carve-out), now gated behind the new `--preview` feature `relocate_trailing_ignore_pragmas` (diff-shades showed the ungated change affects 111 files in the stable corpus, so per the stability policy stable output stays byte-identical to main):

- After a right-hand split, trailing comments on the line's last leaf that match `# <tool>: ignore` (optionally with a bracketed code list) are relocated to the end of the first line of the split. `# type: ignore` is excluded: it has dedicated handling that keeps such lines unsplittable.
- While choosing a split point, invisible (generated) bracket pairs are skipped when the line trails such a pragma on a single physical source line: those splits push the expression to a later line, where a first-line pragma would suppress nothing. This also keeps the FORCE_OPTIONAL_PARENTHESES second opinion from wrapping the expression and moving the pragma off the expression's line (which would oscillate with the deeper-bracket split on the next pass).

```python
# stable (unchanged, pragma is dead)         # --preview (pragma works)
asm_client: SecretsManagerClient = boto3.client(  # pyright: ignore[reportUnknownMemberType]
    "secretsmanager"
)
```

Notes for reviewers:

- The `CHANGES.md` entry lives under "Preview style"; the feature is documented in `docs/the_black_code_style/future_style.md` as `test_feature_lists_are_up_to_date` requires.
- `_over_length_only_due_to_ignore_pragma` repeats the measurement block of the adjacent `_over_length_only_due_to_subscript_comment`. I left that existing function untouched to keep the diff minimal, but can extract a shared helper if preferred.
- Known limitation, discussed with @cobaltt7 below: the first-line placement only helps diagnostics that originate on the first line (typically the callee/statement head); no placement Black can choose covers diagnostics that originate on continuation lines, and tools differ in whether their pragmas are line- or block-scoped.

title: Fix unnecessary line breaks for expressions with comments under preview (#4026, #3713)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #4026
Fixes #3713

### Problem

When a bracketed construct (such as a list literal or function call) contains a standalone comment
before a short expression with operators (binary math, comparisons, comprehensions, etc.), Black
unnecessarily breaks the expression across multiple lines even when it easily fits well within
`--line-length`:

```python
# Before
foobar = [
    # comment
    pathlib.Path("foo")
    / "bar"
    / "baz",
]

fizzbuzz = [
    # comment
    23
    / 7
]

func(
    # comment
    a
    * b
)
```

### Solution

Avoid splitting on delimiters when a preceding standalone comment pushed the line onto its own line
and the expression comfortably fits on a single line.

```py
# After (with --preview)
foobar = [
    # comment
    pathlib.Path("foo") / "bar" / "baz",
]

fizzbuzz = [
    # comment
    23 / 7
]

func(
    # comment
    a * b
)
```

- Added regression tests in tests/data/cases/.
- Ran full test suite and pre-commit checks.

title: Preserve the indentation of indented Jupyter cells
body:
### Description

Black silently dropped the leading whitespace of a Jupyter notebook cell that was
indented on its first code line.

There are two routes to the same result:

- A cell that does not parse on its own has to be masked, and IPython's
  `TransformerManager` dedents whatever it transforms.
- A cell that does parse skips masking, but the formatter still removes the
  leading whitespace.

So all of these cells were rewritten with the indentation stripped:

```python
    x = 1

    if x:
        pass

    # just a comment
```

Formatting a notebook containing any of them rewrote the cell content. Formatting it
again is stable, so this does not show up as an idempotency failure. It just quietly
changes what the user wrote.

`validate_cell` already refuses to touch cells that cannot be safely round tripped,
such as those containing already-transformed magics. This applies the same treatment
to indented cells, whose indentation cannot currently be round tripped.

Cells whose first code line is not indented are unaffected. That includes nested
bodies, which still get formatted:

```python
def f():
  return  1   # -> def f():\n    return 1
```

title: Fix superlinear runtime growth with the number of input files
body:
### Description

Fixes #1951. Full credit for the diagnosis to @asottile's report and @zsol's 2021 profiling: the tight `await asyncio.wait(pending, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` loop in `schedule_formatting` is the culprit — every `asyncio.wait` call re-registers completion callbacks on *all* still-pending tasks, so each completion costs O(pending) bookkeeping, quadratic overall.

This PR replaces the re-wait loop with a single done callback per task that pushes the finished task onto an `asyncio.Queue`, which the loop then consumes. Each completion now costs O(1), results are still processed in completion order, and cancelled/failed task handling, the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers, and cache/report behavior are unchanged.

I didn't use `asyncio.as_completed` (zsol's original suggestion) because on Python 3.10/3.11 it yields wrapper futures rather than the original tasks, and this loop needs the original task to map back to its source path and to inspect `.cancelled()`/`.exception()` — Black still supports those versions.

Benchmarks (Windows 11, Python 3.13.14, editable install, fresh `BLACK_CACHE_DIR` per run, directories of N trivial `x = 1` files, matching the issue's repro shape):

| Files | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 3.45s | 3.13s |
| 10,000 | 67.09s | 18.34s (18.13s second run) |

10x the input now costs 5.9x wall time instead of 19.4x; the remaining sub-linearity is process-pool startup and fixed per-file cost.

Happy to close this in favor of a maintainer's own fix if one is in flight — I searched open/closed PRs and the issue thread and found no competing attempt, but I may have missed something.

title: Fix duplicated comments when string_processing rewrites a line
body:
### Description

Fixes #3665.

With `string_processing` on, an inline comment is printed twice when the transformer strips the parentheses around a string:

```python
a = b.c(
    d,  # comment
    ("e")
)
```

becomes

```python
a = b.c(d, "e")  # comment  # comment
```

The same happens when `StringMerger` removes a backslash continuation from a string on a line that has a comment (`x = "aaa\` / `bbb" + y  # comment`).

`StringParenStripper._transform_to_new_line` and `StringMerger._remove_backslash_line_continuation_chars` both start the new line with `new_line.comments = line.comments.copy()` and then call `append_leaves`. `append_leaves` already re-attaches every comment to the copied leaf, so the new line ends up with each comment twice. One entry is keyed to the new leaf, and one stale entry is keyed to the old leaf, which is no longer in the line. `Line.__str__` renders every value in `comments`, so both copies print.

The fix drops the copy in both places. `StringParenStripper` built its new string leaf by hand and moved that leaf's comments over through the copied map, so it now attaches them with `line.comments_after`, the same way `append_leaves` does. The third `comments.copy()` in `trans.py` (the last line of `StringSplitter`) doesn't call `append_leaves` afterwards, so it is left alone.

`string_processing` is an unstable feature, so the fix needs no new preview flag. Stable and `--preview` output don't change.

Verification:

- The new case `preview_long_strings__duplicate_comments.py` (`--unstable`) fails on `main` (`# comment  # comment` on both lines) and passes with the fix. It lands in its own commit before the fix.
- The full test suite passes: 502 passed, 3 skipped.
- `--unstable` output is byte-identical between `main` and this branch across 20,638 files from the `datasets`, `hermes-agent`, and `llama-index-core` sources (7,728 of them reformatted), so the change only affects lines that hit the duplication.

title: Split only the magic trailing comma's brackets when trailers follow
body:
### Description

Fixes #3268.

When a magic trailing comma is followed by more trailers, Black also splits inside a later trailer:

```python
b = [1,][2](3)
```

becomes

```python
b = [
    1,
][
    2
](3)
```

`right_hand_split_with_omits` tries omit sets from `generate_trailers_to_omit` and takes the first one whose head line fits. For this line the first candidate splits at `[2]`, and its head `b = [1,][` fits. That head still holds the magic trailing comma, so it explodes too, and the split inside `[2]` is wasted. `a = [1,][2]()` escapes the bug only because the empty `()` never produces an omit set of its own.

Under a new preview feature, `fix_magic_trailing_comma_trailer_split`, `right_hand_split_with_omits` skips a candidate whose head still has a magic trailing comma and moves on to the omit set that splits at the comma's own brackets. If no later candidate fits, it falls back to the first skipped one, so lines that only fit that way keep today's output. With the feature on, the example becomes:

```python
b = [
    1,
][2](3)
```

The change sits behind `--preview` because it changes the output for code that Black has already formatted.

Verification:

- The new case `preview_magic_trailing_comma_trailer_split.py` fails on `main` (three of its five lines split inside `[2]`) and passes with the fix. It lands in its own commit before the fix.
- The full test suite passes: 502 passed, 3 skipped.
- `--preview` output is byte-identical before and after the change across 20,731 files from the `datasets`, `hermes-agent`, and `llama-index-core` sources. Stable output does not change.
- pre-commit (isort, flake8, mypy, prettier) passes.

An AI agent (Claude Code) wrote this change and PR description. I'm happy to adjust anything, including the name of the preview feature.

title: Allow whitespace around versions in blackd X-Python-Variant header
body:
### Description

In blackd, comma-separated lists in `X-Python-Variant` with standard whitespace after commas (such as `py3.8, py3.9` or `3.8, py3.9`) and `pyi` with surrounding whitespace failed with HTTP 400 (`Invalid value for X-Python-Variant: expected e.g. '3.7', 'py3.5'`).

For each entry, `parse_python_variant_header` checks `version.startswith("py")` and strips `"py"`, but without stripping whitespace first, an entry like `" py3.9"` retains its leading space, failing `.startswith("py")`. It then extracts `" py3"` as `major_str`, which fails `int()` parsing and raises `InvalidVariantHeader`. Similarly, `" pyi "` failed the exact equality check against `"pyi"`.

This fix strips whitespace from `value` and from each `version` token during iteration, matching the stripping pattern already used for `X-Enable-Unstable-Feature`.

Tests added to `test_blackd_invalid_python_variant`, `test_blackd_pyi`, and `test_blackd_python_variant` covering whitespace variations.

title: fix: keep load-bearing parens on a tuple used as a with item
body:
## Summary

Black rewrote `with ((a, b)):` into `with a, b:`, turning one context manager into two and silently changing what the program does.

`ast.parse` confirms the two forms are different:

- `with ((a, b)):` → `With(items=[withitem(context_expr=Tuple(a, b))])` — **one** item
- `with (a, b):` → `With(items=[withitem(a), withitem(b)])` — **two** items

The original raises `TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support the context manager protocol`; Black's output enters `a` and `b` and runs the body. Black was converting a crashing program into a working one.

## Root cause

`remove_with_parens()` assumes every pair of parentheses in a `with` header is the statement's own optional parens. When the sole context expression is a parenthesized tuple, the extra pair belongs to the *expression*. The function then called `maybe_make_parens_invisible_in_atom(..., remove_brackets_around_comma=True)`, which deliberately bypasses the `max_delimiter_priority_in_atom(node) >= COMMA_PRIORITY` safety check that normally protects comma-bearing parens.

The existing guard at `linegen.py:2182-2186` never fires for these shapes: for a *sole* tuple item there is no comma sibling, and for `with (a, b):` the `with`-parented atom it inspects has no comma siblings either. Instrumenting `is_tuple` showed the clause is effectively dead for these inputs.

## Blast radius

I hand-built 23 variants and AST-compared them: **10 semantic changes before this change, 0 after.** Broken before: `with ((a,b)):`, `with ((a,b), c):`, `with (c, (a,b)):`, `with ((a,b),(c,d)):`, `with (((a,b))):`, `with ((a,)):`, `with ((lambda: 1, 2)):`, `with ((a,b),):`, and the `async with` forms.

## The change

`remove_with_parens` now bails out when the atom holds a load-bearing tuple, and a helper documents why:

```python
if _holds_load_bearing_tuple(node.children[1]) or (
    is_tuple(node) and parent.type != syms.with_stmt
):
    return
```

Two details were not obvious and are worth calling out:

- **Both** paren pairs must survive, not just the inner one. `format_str` runs a forced second pass that re-parses the first pass's text, so fixing only the CST still emitted the intermediate `with (a, b):`, which the second pass then re-parsed as two context managers. Bailing out at the container level is what makes the output round-trip.
- **The walrus exemption is required, not cosmetic.** `tests/data/cases/pep_572_remove_parens.py:65` deliberately asserts `with ((x := await a, y := await b)):` collapses to one layer, and those two forms really are identical, because parentheses are mandatory around a bare named expression in a with-item. Without the exemption that test fails. I hit exactly that on the first attempt.

## Tests

New fixture `tests/data/cases/tuple_as_only_contextmanager.py`, auto-discovered by `test_simple_format` via `all_data_cases("cases")`. It covers the sole tuple, mixed items on both sides, multiple tuple items, triply-nested parens, `async with`, and `with (a, b):` as a control proving the legitimate simplification still happens.

- Before: 6 cases wrong, test fails. After: passes.
- `pytest tests/test_format.py -q` → 250 passed.
- `pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/test_format.py --ignore=tests/test_blackd.py` → 217 passed, 3 skipped.
- `black --check src/black/linegen.py` clean.

`for ((a, b)) in x:` → `for a, b in x:` looks alarming but is not a bug: the for-target grammar treats both forms identically and the ASTs match.

I confirmed this is unfixed upstream — `main` still has the identical three-line guard.

title: Keep the CRLF ending of the line skipped by `--skip-source-first-line`
body:
### Description

With `-x` / `--skip-source-first-line`, `format_file_in_place` reads the skipped first line as raw bytes and prepends it to the formatted code. It then writes the result through `open(..., newline=newline)`, which turns every `\n` into the file's newline. On a CRLF file the header already ends in `\r\n`, so it comes out as `\r\r\n`. Only the first line is affected, and only when the rest of the file changes.

`-x` mirrors Python's `-x` option, which exists for the Windows batch-file trick, so CRLF files are exactly where it gets used.

```console
$ printf 'hdr ((\r\nx  =  1\r\n' > t.py
$ black -q -x t.py; od -c t.py
0000000   h   d   r       (   (  \r  \r  \n   x       =       1  \r  \n
```

`--diff` goes through the same newline translation, so the header context line in the diff also shows up as `hdr ((\r\r\n`.

The fix gives the header a plain `\n` ending when it already ends in the file's newline, so the translation turns it back into the original ending. The other cases stay as they were, including `test_skip_source_first_line_when_mixing_newlines` (a CRLF header followed by LF code).

title: Keep dictionary keys with operators together in preview (#3442)
body:
### Summary of Changes

    When a dictionary key contains operators (such as `+`, `-`, or `%`) and the line exceeds the line length, `delimiter_split`
    would previously split inside the key at the operator instead of allowing the dictionary value to wrap or explode onto a   new line.

    This PR introduces the preview style feature `keep_dict_keys_with_operators`:
    - Checks if a line is a dictionary entry whose highest-priority delimiters are located on the key side (before the bracket depth-0 colon).
    - Defers `delimiter_split` to `right_hand_split` when the key and the opening parenthesis/bracket of the value fit within the line length limit.
    - Leaves keys that are genuinely too long by themselves to split inside the key as before.
    - Adds comprehensive preview tests, updates schema, documentation in `future_style.md`, and changelog in `CHANGES.md`.

 ### Example

    ```python
    # Before
    tests = {
        Timestamp("2014-07-04 15:00")
        + Nano(5): this_is_a_very_long_function("2014-07-04 16:00"),
    }

    # After (with --preview)
    tests = {
        Timestamp("2014-07-04 15:00") + Nano(5): this_is_a_very_long_function(
            "2014-07-04 16:00"
        ),
    }

title: Don't wrap part of an unmerged implicit string concatenation in parens
body:
### Description

Fixes #3855

With string processing enabled (`--unstable`), Black produces code it can't parse when the value of a keyword argument, a lambda body or an `else` branch is an implicit concatenation that StringMerger won't merge, e.g. raw strings:

```console
$ printf "dict(a=r' ' r'')\n" > foo.py
$ black -l 1 --unstable foo.py
error: cannot parse: foo.py:5:4
        r""
       ^
ParseError: bad input
```

The same happens at the default line length when the first string is too long, e.g. `some_function_name(argument=r"<long string>" r" more")`.

StringMerger refuses raw strings (`StringMerger does NOT merge raw strings.`), so the concatenation stays split and the earlier delimiter split puts `a=r" "` and `r""` on separate lines. StringParenWrapper then gets the line `a=r" "` on its own. `_assign_match` (and `_dict_or_lambda_match` / `_else_match`) only look at the leaves in the current line, so they match, and the wrapper turns it into:

```python
dict(
    a=(
        r" "
    )
    r""
)
```

This PR wraps the whole concatenation in parens instead:

```python
dict(
    a=(
        r" "
        r""
    )
)
```

That is also what `--unstable` already does for concatenations it can merge (`argument=(` with the merged string split inside).

- `linegen.py`: for a line inside brackets whose only delimiters are between implicitly concatenated strings and which doesn't start with a string (`a=STRING STRING`, `lambda: STRING STRING`, `else STRING STRING`), `string_paren_wrap` is tried before `delimiter_split`. If it doesn't match, `delimiter_split` runs next as before.
- `trans.py`: `_assign_match` and `_dict_or_lambda_match` skip strings concatenated with the matched one (`_else_match` already accepted anything after the string), so the wrapper puts the whole concatenation inside the parens. `do_splitter_match` declines when the first string already fits on the line or the line has comments, so those lines are still split at the concatenation as before. It also still refuses a string whose next sibling is a `STRING` on another line, as a fallback for the cases that don't take this path (e.g. a comment between the strings).

I added three cases to `preview_long_strings__regression.py` (keyword argument, lambda, `else` branch) at the default line length, plus one where the first string fits exactly on the line, which `main` already formats without parens and which must stay that way. With upstream `main`'s `trans.py` and `linegen.py` the test fails with `black.parsing.InvalidInput: cannot parse: 702:4`. With them, it passes.

To check that output which didn't crash before is unchanged, I formatted the inputs in `tests/data/cases/`, the files in `src/black/`, and 6636 generated implicit concatenations (raw, bytes, f-string and plain prefixes; keyword arguments, dict values, lambdas, `else`, `return`, assignments, call arguments, with and without comments) in stable, `--preview` and `--unstable` mode at line lengths 88, 40, 20 and 1, with `main` and with this branch. None of the 83268 runs changed output. 4479 runs that crash on `main` now format, all under `--unstable`.

Validation (Windows, Python 3.12):

- `pre-commit run` on the changed files: isort, flake8, mypy, prettier and the other hooks pass

title: Add --cache-dir command-line option
body:
### Description

Add a `--cache-dir` option so callers can configure Black cache storage without setting an environment variable. The command-line option takes precedence over `BLACK_CACHE_DIR` and works for both single-file and concurrent formatting.

The selected path now covers both formatting caches and blib2to3 grammar caches. Import-time grammar initialization is write-free until Click resolves the effective cache directory, so an explicit CLI path does not touch the environment/default cache.

Closes #5174

title: Fix unclosed file handles in Converter.parse_graminit_h/_c
body:
## What

`blib2to3.pgen2.conv.Converter.parse_graminit_h` and `.parse_graminit_c` each open the grammar `.h`/`.c` file with a bare `f = open(filename)` and then read from `f` for the rest of the function (a `for line in f:` loop in the `_h` case, direct `next(f)` calls throughout the `_c` case). Neither method ever closes the handle — no `with`, no matching `.close()`, no `finally`.

Found via [codehound](https://github.com/kratos0718/codehound), a static analyzer I built; this repo's copy of `blib2to3` was part of a broader scan.

## Fix

Read the file's lines up front inside a `with` block, then operate on the resulting list instead of the file object directly:

- `parse_graminit_h`: `for line in f` → `for line in lines`, where `lines` comes from `with open(filename) as f: lines = f.readlines()`.
- `parse_graminit_c`: same idea, but wrapped in `iter(...)` since the rest of the function drives itself entirely through `next(f)` calls (the existing comment even calls this out: `# The code below essentially uses f's iterator-ness!`) — `f = iter(fh.readlines())` preserves that unchanged.

Both changes are scoped to the `open(...)` line and the following loop header only; the parsing logic itself (all the regex matching, asserts, and table-building in the ~160-line `parse_graminit_c` body) is untouched, so the diff stays minimal per the norm from #3363/#3794.

## Testing

`Converter` isn't currently exercised by any test in this repo (nothing else in the tree imports it — it looks like a standalone pgen-output-loading utility), so I built a synthetic pgen-format `.h`/`.c` fixture pair and drove both methods through it directly:

- `parse_graminit_h` / `parse_graminit_c` both reproduce the exact same `symbol2number`/`number2symbol`/`dfas`/`labels`/`states`/`start` results as before the change, for a minimal one-symbol grammar.
- The error path (nonexistent file) still returns `False` and prints the same message.
- A descriptor-count check before/after a successful parse confirms the handle is actually released now.

Also ran `python -c "import blib2to3.pgen2.conv"` to confirm no syntax/import issues.

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` in a decorated function group in stubs
body:
### Description

With `--preview --pyi`, `# fmt: skip` on a function that follows another decorated function of the same name crashes Black:

```python
from typing import overload

@overload
def f(x: int) -> int: ...
@overload
def f(x: str) -> str: ...  # fmt: skip
```

```
error: cannot format demo.pyi: 
```

The message is empty because it's a bare `AssertionError`. The same happens for methods, for a property setter after its getter, and for `async def`, which fails with an `IndexError` instead.

**Cause.** The `pyi_overload_group_blank_lines` feature (#5021) reads a function's name in `_get_funcdef_name()` as `funcdef.children[1]` and asserts that it's a leaf. `# fmt: skip` has already turned the leaves of the skipped line into a standalone comment, so that child is something else:

```
funcdef
  STANDALONE_COMMENT 'def f(x: str) -> str: ...  # fmt: skip'
  parameters   (0 children)
  simple_stmt
```

The empty `parameters` node is what #5429 removes. With that change `children[1]` is the `simple_stmt`, so this crash stays; the two fixes are independent.

**Fix.** Return `None` when there is no `NAME` to read. The skipped function is then not treated as part of the group, and the blank lines around it are left as the stable style has them. I didn't try to recover the name from the comment text.

**Tests.** `tests/data/cases/pyi_overload_groups_fmt_skip.py` covers a function, `async def`, a method and a property setter. It fails on `main` with the `AssertionError` and passes here, and the full suite passes.

I found this with the same mutation fuzzer as #5429. With both changes applied, `# fmt: skip` on each line of a few overload and property groups, and `# fmt: off`/`on` around each range of lines, format with the safety checks passing in `--pyi --preview`, `--pyi` and `--preview`.

title: Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` one-line definitions with type parameters
body:
### Description

`# fmt: skip` on a one-line function or class with PEP 695 type parameters crashes Black:

```python
def f[T](): pass  # fmt: skip
```

```
error: cannot format ...: list index out of range
```

The same happens for `class C[T]: pass`, `async def`, methods, and the `*Ts` / `**P` forms. It's a regression from #4552, which started honouring `# fmt: skip` on one-liner functions: 25.1.0 formats these, and 25.9.0 through 26.5.1 crash.

**Cause.** The backward walk in `_generate_ignored_nodes_from_fmt_skip` collects the leaves on the skipped line one at a time, descending into `typeparams` and `parameters`. Converting those leaves into the standalone comment leaves the emptied nodes behind:

```
funcdef
  STANDALONE_COMMENT 'def f[T](): pass  # fmt: skip'
  typeparams   (0 children)
  parameters   (0 children)
```

`visit_typeparams` then runs `node.children[0].prefix = ""` on an empty node. `parameters` is left empty as well; nothing indexes into it, so it just happens not to crash.

**Fix.** When the walk climbs out of a node whose children are all already ignored, take the node itself instead of its leaves. Children collapsed on an earlier climb are already nodes by then, so the check compares children rather than leaves; `[T: int]` needs that, since its `typevar` collapses before `typeparams` does. I fixed it in the walk rather than guarding the three visitors because the empty nodes are the underlying problem, and it's where #5161 and #5311 fixed their `fmt: skip` crashes.

**Tests.** `tests/data/cases/fmtskip_type_params.py` covers the plain, `*Ts`, `**P`, bounded and combined forms, `async def`, classes and a method. It fails on `main` with the `IndexError` and passes here, and the full suite passes.

Since this changes a walk every `# fmt: skip` goes through, I also ran a mutation fuzzer over `tests/data/cases` before and after the change: it inserts `# fmt: skip`, `# fmt: off`/`on`, comments and magic trailing commas, and checks each variant in the same four modes `assert_format` uses. The only difference between the two runs is these four `IndexError` cases going away.

title: Return HTTP 400 for an empty `X-Python-Variant` entry in blackd
body:
### Description

The blackd docs say an invalid value in any of the request headers gets an `HTTP 400` response that names the problematic header. `X-Python-Variant` breaks that for three kinds of value:

- an empty value;
- a bare `py`;
- a list with an empty entry, such as a trailing comma (`3.6,`) or a doubled comma (`py3.6,,py3.7`).

For each entry, `parse_python_variant_header` strips an optional `py` prefix and then reads `version[0]` outside its `try` block. An empty entry therefore raises `IndexError`, which escapes the header validation, so the handler logs a traceback and answers with `HTTP 500` and the body `string index out of range`.

The fix rejects an empty entry with the same `InvalidVariantHeader` the function already raises for other malformed values. The request now gets the documented 400: `Invalid value for X-Python-Variant: expected e.g. '3.7', 'py3.5'`.

The four values above are added to `test_blackd_invalid_python_variant`. The test fails with `500 != 400` before the change and passes after it.

title: Fix ValueError in find_project_root for files on multiple Windows drives (#5379)
body:
Resolves #5379.

    **Description:**
    When passing sources located on completely different Windows drives (e.g., `black C:\app\a.py D:\tmp\b.py`), `find_project_root` computes the common parents of all input paths. Because paths on separate Windows drives have no common `Path` parent, the resulting set intersection is empty. Previously, passing this empty intersection to `max()` caused an unhandled `ValueError` crash.

    This PR fixes the crash by checking if the intersection is empty before calling `max()`. If there is no common base (as is the
  case with files on different drives), it gracefully falls back to using the resolved current working directory (`Path.cwd()`) as
  the base to search for configuration files like `pyproject.toml`.

    **Changes:**
    - Updated `src/black/files.py` to handle an empty parent intersection and fallback to `Path.cwd()`.
    - Added `test_find_project_root_multiple_drives` regression test in `tests/test_black.py` (skipped on non-Windows platforms).

title: Remove unnecessary parentheses in unpacking targets (#3080)
body:
## Summary

    Fixes #3080.

    Black previously removed outer parentheses around tuples in unpacking targets (e.g. `for (a, b) in c:` -> `for a, b in c:`),

    2. Preserves syntactically meaningful parentheses (nested tuples/lists like `(b, c)`, single-element tuples `(b,)`, annotated targets, and walrus expressions).

title: Don't require sys.stdout.buffer when writing formatted output or diffs
body:
### Description

Fixes #2516

**Bug:** Calling `black.reformat_code()` / `black.format_stdin_to_stdout()` from a Jupyter notebook fails with `AttributeError: 'OutStream' object has no attribute 'buffer'`. The diff output of `format_file_in_place()` (`WriteBack.DIFF` / `COLOR_DIFF`) has the same problem.

**Root cause:** Both functions wrap `sys.stdout.buffer` in `io.TextIOWrapper` so they can control the encoding and newline translation. `TextIOBase.buffer` is [not part of the `TextIOBase` API](https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.TextIOBase.buffer) and ipykernel's `OutStream` doesn't have it. `format_stdin_to_stdout()` builds that wrapper in its `finally` block for every `write_back` mode, so even `--check`-style calls crash. The issue thread notes that just using `getattr(sys.stdout, "buffer", sys.stdout)` doesn't work either, because `OutStream.write()` only accepts `str`.

**Change:** Both code paths now go through a small `_write_to_stdout()` helper:

- If `sys.stdout` has a `buffer`, it does what the code did before: wraps it in `io.TextIOWrapper(..., write_through=True)`, wraps it for Windows colors where needed, writes, then detaches.
- If there is no `buffer`, it writes text straight to `sys.stdout`. It does the `\n` -> `newline` translation itself (this is what `TextIOWrapper` would do, and the content has already been normalized to `\n` at that point) and leaves encoding to the stream. The stream is never detached or closed.

`format_stdin_to_stdout()` now only touches stdout when `write_back` is `YES`/`DIFF`/`COLOR_DIFF`. `wrap_stream_for_windows()`'s annotation is widened from `io.TextIOWrapper` to `TextIO` so it accepts `sys.stdout`. At runtime it already accepted any stream.

**Tests:** I added three tests that patch `sys.stdout` with an `io.StringIO`, which has no `buffer` and only accepts `str` (like `OutStream`). They cover `format_stdin_to_stdout` with `YES`/`CHECK`/`NO`/`DIFF`/`COLOR_DIFF`, `reformat_code`, and the `format_file_in_place` diff path with both `\n` and `\r\n` files. All three failed with the `AttributeError` before the fix and pass after it.

Validation (macOS, Python 3.14):
- `pytest -n auto tests`: 484 passed, 3 skipped
- `pre-commit run -a`: everything passes except mypy, which reports an `action/main.py:60` `tomllib` error that also shows up on unmodified `main` in my environment. It has nothing to do with this change, and there are no mypy errors in the touched files.
- `black --check` on the changed files: clean

title: Fix `# fmt: skip` on the opening bracket of an if/while/for/with header
body:
### Description

Fixes #5402.

On `main`, `if (  # fmt: skip` followed by a multi-line condition fails with `InvalidInput: cannot parse`. `while (`, `for i in (` and `with (` fail the same way. 26.5.1 formats all of these.

When `# fmt: skip` sits on the opening bracket, the whole `if ( ... )` gets turned into one `STANDALONE_COMMENT` leaf, and the line is just that leaf plus `:`. `right_hand_split` finds nothing to split, so the line falls through to `_force_standalone_comment_split` from #5144. That function splits after every standalone comment, which puts the `:` on its own line, and the second pass can't parse it.

The split after a standalone comment only matters when the comment would swallow the code after it. A real standalone comment always does. Code converted by `fmt: skip` only does if its last line ends in a comment, and here it ends in `)`. So the split after a standalone comment now only happens when its last line contains `#`. Code with a `#` inside a string on that last line still gets split, so those cases behave exactly as they do today.

The paired form from #5397 (`# fmt: skip` on both the opening line and the `):` line) still fails after this change. It's a different path, and #5401 covers it.

Implemented with Claude Code; I reviewed and tested the change.
